Mr. Speaker, subject to Standing Order 36 it is my pleasure and honour to present a petition signed by several hundred residents of Alberta in Edmonton, Calgary and Red Deer dealing with the utter tragedy going on in Bosnia-Hercegovina.
I will just give the substance of the petition as it is very short. The petition states that innocent men, women and children who are ill-equipped to defend themselves continue to be slaughtered in Bosnia-Hercegovina and Croatia by heavily armed aggressors.
The petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to demand that the UN take immediate military action to stop the fighting. Failing that they request the UN arms embargo be lifted so that the victims in Bosnia-Hercegovina and Croatia can be properly equipped to defend themselves. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Question No. 453 will be answered today.

With respect to the total number of contracts awarded to the private sector for consulting services by the Canadian International Development Agency (CIDA), (a) what are the selection criteria (b) how many were awarded to each province during the past five fiscal years?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister for External Relations and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie; Minister of State (Seniors)
speechtext:
With respect to the total number of contracts awarded to the private sector for consulting services by the Canadian International Development Agency, the detailed answer is as follows:
(a) Selection Criteria
A unique set of criteria is established for each selection which reflects the particular requirements of the assignment to be contracted. In broad terms, these criteria normally include:
1.	Professional and Technical Expertise: this might include the requirement for a professional designation or accreditation (i.e. chartered accountant, engineer, agronomist) specializing in a particular field (i.e. a chartered accountant specializing in the establishment credit systems for small or medium sized firms; or an electrical engineer specializing in alternative sources of heating such as biomass, or new and renewable energy).
Note: CIDA classifies its professional and technical requirements in some 700 different sectors, subsectors and areas of specialization.
2.	Experience: might include the number of years of practical experience in a given field; experience in doing similar work-planning, execution, monitoring, evaluation-under similar conditions; international, regional or country-specific experience.
3.	Language Capability: The language preference of the recipient country (usually English or French) is the determining factor. There are sometimes requirements for other special language skills, such as Spanish, Portuguese, Mandarin.
4.	Availability: This refers to the availability of the recommended consultant to provide the services within a specific time frame i.e to attend a scheduled international forum; to be a member of organized mission team.
5.	Cost: In keeping with government contracting policies and practices, CIDA seeks to obtain the best value for the Crown (best services at a fair market price).

That this House condemns the government for policies regarding jobs and job creation, post-secondary education and job training and retraining that are having the effect of robbing a whole generation of young Canadians of their legitimate aspirations.
Ele said: Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to speak on our opposition day motion today:
That this House condemns the government for policies regarding jobs and job creation, post-secondary education and job training and retraining that are having the effect of robbing a whole generation of young Canadians of their legitimate aspirations.
Undoubtedly a crisis faces young Canadians today which this country can no longer afford and we as
Supply
members of Parliament can no longer afford to relegate these youth issues to the bottom of the political agenda. For this reason, I welcome the opportunity that this opposition day motion gives us. It allows us to bring to light many of the problems facing these young Canadians.
I would like to begin by putting a question to my colleagues on the other side. How many times have we heard that young Canadians are this country's greatest asset and our greatest resource, that they represent the future? Unfortunately our future, the youth of this country, have lost hope. They are demoralized. They are marginalized. They are a lost generation. They are generation x.
The problems facing young people in Canada today are overwhelming: acute unemployment of close to 18 per cent; fears over job security and changing labour requirements; drastic cuts to education; inadequate skills to cope with increasingly technological change and a knowledge based economy; over a 30 per cent high school drop-out rate; a dramatic increase in the number of street kids; drugs and sexually transmitted diseases; and finally, a lack of direction or coherent government policies to deal with these problems.
The youth of this country feel lost and alone and they are tired of government inaction. They know what the problems are and they know what the solutions are. The time for action is now.
Chronic youth unemployment and under-employment has demoralized the young people of this country. In fact the biggest problem facing youth today is unemployment. As a country, we need to give back to Canadians purpose and hope. We need to get them back to work.
Unfortunately there is a present void in our government's youth policy in this area. Why? Because the government has never explicitly stated a specific policy geared to putting youth back to work. In other words, they have no game plan to get Canadians working again.
I believe that for young people today, no other policy program is more important than getting them a first job. We know that on-the-job experience is a critical part of developing marketable labour and skills. Of course, the problems facing young Canadians today is that they have not been able to get that first job. Otherwise, they tend to be marginalized until there remains but one big question: How do we get young Canadians working again? How do they get that all-important first job? How do we give them back that hope and confidence and let them know that this country cares about their future?

March 18, 1993
Supply
In the short term, young people can be put to work. They can be put to work to do environmental and community based service. A Canadian environmental youth corps would give young people the opportunity to participate in environmental rehabilitation and education projects. I feel this would be an investment, not only in our youth but in our communities which are today suffering. To give young people career experience, summer employment opportunities must be maintained by the government. In fact, the government must acknowledge that giving youth summer job experience is an investment in our future.
Since 1985 the Challenge program which has provided summer job opportunities has been slashed by more than half. In 1985 it was $205 million, today it is $101.9 million.
Shame, shame.

Mr. Speaker, if we are serious about any future jobs for our young Canadians, we need to give more importance to these summer job experiences and first-time jobs for students.
What about the long term? What are the long-term prospects for our Canadian youth? What are the challenges that this country, especially its young people, face going into the next century? The fact is that this country is undergoing extensive restructuring as world economies become increasingly integrated. We are told that we must face globalization, that we must be ready for change.
Therefore, the greatest challenge facing Canada and Canadians will be to become more competitive and a more innovative country. However, as this country has been slow to respond to this international challenge it represents more of a problem for today's youth, both in the short and the long term.
The biggest problem facing youth today is unemployment, specifically structural unemployment. This means that the demand for labour is changing faster than the supply of labour can adapt. This is problematic for our young people because although there is demand for high-tech, high-skilled jobs, young people do not have the training for these jobs and they cannot compete.
It stands to reason that until we give our young people the tools they need in order to compete, they will be condemned to remain in the marginal aspects. They will remain marginal workers taking temporary, low-skilled and low-paying jobs with little job security. Imagine the feeling of low self-esteem resulting from being chronically unemployed. It is ironic, is it not? The future of this country, our youth, feel that they have no future.
We should not lose sight of the implications of high youth unemployment, both on the victims and on Canada's future competitiveness. How do we become more competitive? How do we change the mind-set of a country that seems slow to adapt to this change? How do we encourage Canadians to embrace the technology of an information economy as opposed to resources and manufacturing?
In my opinion, education and continuing education is the basis of a productive and competitive society. If we want to compete globally we must place a high priority on education. Canada's commitment to education must be unequivocal. It is fair to say that our poor economy and our future prospects are tied to the quality of our education system. Therefore, a revamped education system must be ready to give young people better job-related training to help them beat the vicious cycle of structural unemployment.
First, some fundamental problems must be addressed, and these problems are obvious. Federal government cuts in transfers to the provinces have left provincial treasuries empty with little choice but to make drastic cuts in important areas such as education. Within the school system teaching must be ready to adapt to the many changes that are going to take place over the next decade.
We also have to acknowledge that two-thirds of graduating high school students do not go on to university or to post-secondary education. This represents a large pool of untapped resources that do not see conventional post-secondary education as a viable option. Because our secondary schools are oriented toward academic subjects and because our school system does not encourage vocational programs, there are thousands and thousands of students who feel that they have been given no practical alternatives within this system. This represents a tragic waste of .potential.
March 18, 1993

Only about 10 per cent of students are enrolled in apprenticeship programs. Moreover, the present apprenticeship program system is highly concentrated in manufacturing and construction trades, instead of meeting the growing demands of the technological revolution.
Between 1996 and the year 2000 the percentage of the work force requiring high-skilled jobs is going to increase from 45 per cent to 64 per cent. However, the percentage of Canadians actually acquiring high-skilled training is declining. Think about it. We are simply not prepared for the next century. It is today's young people, the youth of this country who are going to suffer.
Therefore, in order to effectively target educational resources and new and changing demands in government, we must create a national apprenticeship training program. This would enable our young people to acquire the specialized fields they are going to need for the jobs of tomorrow, something that universities today do not seem to be able to provide.
A change in the educational system must also include an extension of co-operative education. A promoted and expanded co-operative education program would bring together government, business and labour to give these young people a career experience that is essential for their futures.
Moreover co-operative education, besides giving valuable work experience, provides students with the ability to finance their education and it is therefore cost effective for governments. It also gives youth opportunity to understand their discipline and to improve their ties within the corporate community. For government, co-op education gives all partners-government, business, labour and our local communities-a chance to work together in the best interests of Canada's young people. As we become more competitive we must learn how to consult and to collaborate with one another.
Obviously there is a correlation between education, the quality of the labour market and the performance of our economy. For this reason government along with all players must act quickly because the education system in
Supply
this country is simply not ready for the changes and the challenges of tomorrow.
I would like to take a moment to talk about the unique challenges of rural youth. It has become apparent to all Canadians that small rural communities across this country are in a state of decline. It includes fishing communities in Newfoundland, it includes farming communities all over Canada, including my riding of Haldimand-Norfolk and other resource based towns.
Sadly, rural Canada increasingly cannot retain its young people. Rural youth feel that they have no choice but to leave their homes and to leave their communities. In many cases the education system can be blamed for the way that it socializes people off the farm or away from the fishing community. Of course many young Canadians leave their communities with the hope of finding jobs. Unfortunately high unemployment is both an urban and a rural problem and even when they leave these homes they do not seem to find jobs.
As I have already noted, education skills experience is needed for most of today's jobs. Many young people from rural communities end up on the streets. In fact, we were told in our task force hearings across the country that one-third of the homeless youth in urban centres come from small town Canada. They come out of small towns and end up on the streets of these urban centres.
The point is that we on all sides of this House from all parts of Canada must consider very seriously the crisis facing rural Canada and the implications of a decaying rural infrastructure and the effect that has on our rural youth. We have to come together and develop strategies to deal with this.
It is time for all Canadians to realize that rural Canada is a vital and an integral part of a strong and united Canada. We cannot afford to lose our young people.
Government is always key to restoring hope to a country hit hard by tough economic times. It is government that must take a leadership role. The private sector has been slow to respond and to adapt to the changes facing this country. I believe in the short term government can be the engine of economic growth because government sets an example for the rest of the country.

March 18, 1993
Supply
If we want Canadians to start spending again, if we want the private sector to be ready for the challenges of globalization and if we want to show young Canadians that we care about their future, then we have to show them that government is willing to act and take the initiative.
Government should not have to apologize for discriminate spending in this area because fiscal responsibility means more than just slashing and cutting. It means more than just a bottom line because once this country, especially its young people, loses confidence and hope then bottom-line fiscal policy means very little. For young Canadians the prospect of a strong economy restores the sense of confidence in what their country can do for them, both in the long and the short term.
Young people are worried. They are also worried about the deficit and debt reduction. After all, they are the ones who are going to have to deal with them. I do concede that there is a temptation within governments to indiscriminately spend, and this must be tempered by fiscal responsibility and a consideration of our long-term goals and objectives.
However, I maintain that the best way to restore hope in young Canadians is to give them back their lost sense of pride, their confidence and their self-esteem. To get them working again is to empower them and to give them back all they have lost.
All Canadians, not just government, must take more seriously these challenges facing young Canadians. Governments must work co-operatively with, each other, business, labour and local communities to develop these policies and programs geared toward young people.
Working co-operatively means pulling together to find constructive solutions. Instead of arguing about who is to blame we have to concentrate on constructive ways to solve this problem and get young Canadians working again, because young Canadians need solutions now.
If we continue to ignore the problems of generation x we risk losing the unlimited potential of an entire generation of Canadians. We have to be willing to invest in our future. We have to give young Canadians a renewed sense of hope and confidence. After all, this is our future we are talking about.

Mr. Speaker, I understand that Germany produces 400,000 apprenticeships a year. I think Canada produces 24,000. Could the member make some comments as to how we might try to catch up to Germany and start to do more for youth who are not, for one reason or another, able to go to university or pursue post-secondary education?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for that question. He does bring to light one of the examples that we have seen as we have studied this issue across the country. We went across this country and talked to all Canadians about it. A number of people mentioned the German experience.
The real fact of the matter is that Germany creates more of these jobs for almost half of the money we spend in this country. It not only has more apprenticeship spots, it not only has people who come out of this system trained not only in the construction or manufacturing trades but in those jobs of the future such as the high-tech and biotech areas, but it does so for half the money we spend.
We as a country need to seriously examine this area because it is money well spent. It is an investment in our young people, and it is an investment that does not cost Canadians a lot of money.

Mr. Speaker, there are approximately 960,000 small businesses in this country right now. They represent the greatest hope for new job creation because most of the larger corporations are downsizing and restructuring. I know that the minister responsible for small businesses supports this position.
I would like to ask the hon. member a question in light of the fact that there are so many of these small businesses right now struggling to make ends meet and stay viable, and many of the entrepreneurs who are operating these small businesses are working 70 to 80 hours a week and sometimes six or seven days a week, while at the same time there are close to 400,000 young people, some of whom have just graduated from school, who are basically sitting at home because there is not a lot of job opportunities out there and so we are disbursing close to $8 billion to $10 billion through unemployment insurance and welfare.
March 18, 1993

Would it not be a much better approach to try to link the job creation program for youth directly to the small business sector? The person working with the small business person would be learning a skill. That person would be learning a craft, a trade or some sense of business practice and entrepreneurship. Would it not be a much better approach to link those people who are unemployed with the small business sector of this country?
For probably an extra couple of thousand dollars on top of what we are already paying in welfare we would not only be giving people this new skill and opportunity but would also be returning their dignity to them.
I wonder if our party's critic for youth could respond to that.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for his input. He is always talking about small business and this is one of the areas in which small business can play a key role.
We do allow small businesses to have students through the SEED program, albeit the money has been cut off in that area. The hon. member knows, because he brought this to my attention, that small businesses are the people who are training Canadians today. We could increase the money going into training because it would help young Canadians by giving them their first job experience and it would help small businesses by giving them trained people and people to help them.
I know the hon. member knows this, but I want to bring to the House's attention that a 1991 report by the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology said that the average Canadian worker currently receives only seven hours of training annually. Compare that to 17 hours in Australia, 170 hours in Sweden, or 200 hours in Japan; and we are wondering why we are lagging behind in this country.
It is not small business that is lagging behind because it is doing its fair share. Both government and big business in this country are going to have to sit down and address not only the needs of Canadian youth being trained but the needs of businesses for the future.
It is they that lack these people with training. There is a complete lack of training in jobs, the government says so itself. It says that there are thousands of jobs that
Supply
cannot be filled because Canadians are not trained for those jobs.
The time is now. Germany, for instance, has within the last three years increased its funding in this area by some 45 per cent while we in Canada have slashed ours. Germany knows the answer. Japan knows the answer. Sweden knows the answer. It is time this country did what was right and discovered the answer.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Minister of State (Youth) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that we have a very serious subject to discuss here today.
I thank the hon. member for raising the issue. Of course I do not agree with the wording of the motion as it was put by the hon. member. I could be tempted to underline that I sense a little partisanship in the wording, but notwithstanding that I believe it is an important subject worth discussion in this House.
And you've never been partisan?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Absolutely not, but I am thinking about it. That being said, it is important to raise these issues and to discuss them.
The wording of the motion gives the impression that this government has done absolutely nothing with respect to the youth situation in Canada. I regret that my hon. friend has taken that slant, which is that nothing has been done and consequently it is a desperate situation. I do not think it is an ideal situation but it is certainly not a desperate one.
The best way for me to respond to such a wrongly worded motion is to review a few of the things we are doing to help young Canadians. I know that my time is limited and I will not be able to touch on all the subjects, but I am sure that my colleagues who will be addressing this important question today will complete the list of programs and initiatives of this government with respect to youth in Canada.
Let me begin by pointing out that despite the tough economic conditions that we have been experiencing the
17.8	per cent youth unemployment rate in 1992, which is totally unacceptable, was below the historical high of
19.8	per cent in 1983 when by coincidence my friend's party formed the government.

March 18, 1993
Supply
The gap between the general unemployment rate and the youth unemployment rate is lower now than it was between 1981 and 1982, also a period of Liberal government.
As well, the youth unemployment rate fell to 16.7 per cent last month at a time when there were 4,000 more young Canadians active in the labour force than in the previous month. This was the result of strong employment growth and a decline in unemployment.

Employment and Immigration Canada knows the employment situation in this country better than anyone and it also knows better than anyone how to help young Canadians find their feet in a rapidly changing labour market.
We know that two-thirds of all jobs created in Canada during this decade will require a level of education beyond Grade 12. We know that 40 per cent of these jobs will require at least five years of post-secondary education. Nevertheless, we know that nevertheless, more than 100,000 young people drop out of high school every year. This represents a national dropout rate of about 30 per cent.
So what are we doing about it? Let us look at some of the ways in which Employment and Immigration Canada tries to help the young people of this country.

The first step in preparing for employment is a good education. We launched a five-year $296.4 million stay-in-school initiative, which is now concluding its fourth year of operation. Stay-in-school is a national dropout prevention strategy comprising three components: public awareness, mobilization of stakeholders, and programs and services.
Stay in school programs and services aimed at young people at risk of dropping out are delivered under START. Funded under the national stay-in-school initiative, the START option provides funding for a variety of labour market programs and services designed to keep high school students from dropping out.
Business, community organizations, municipal governments, public health or education institutions and band
councils all co-operate with Employment and Immigration Canada in START initiatives.
START activities include many innovative approaches aimed at giving young participants life skills training, personal financial management ability and work experience.

Because we must keep working at reducing this 30 per cent dropout rate-even during the summer holidays- about 420 student employment centres are open during the summer. This year we will celebrate the twenty-fifth anniversary of the centres, which were created to help young people find summer jobs.
Canada Employment Centres for Students help students find jobs and they help employers find workers. The staff in these centres are university students themselves. Their job is to offer students the practical guidance they need to find a job, including advice on how to look for work, draft a curriculum vitae and prepare for an interview.
Canada Employment Centres for Students also offer information on various federal and provincial programs. In 1992 the centres made more than 171,500 placements across the country. In addition, more than 106,200 people took advantage of information sessions organized by the centres.
The Canada Employment Centres for Students also help employers. The centres offer direct access to placement and posting services as well as information on remuneration levels, federal and provincial legislation and programs for young people, and information on the number of students available.
We are understandably proud of our efforts and success in this field.

Take the challenge program which has helped tens of thousands of students locate summer employment since 1985. Challenge helps students gain practical work experience that will assist them to make the transition from school to work. It encourages employers to create jobs and to sponsor on-the-job training for young people.
March 18, 1993

Challenge '93 will maintain a strong link to the national stay- in-school initiative. It focuses on helping those who have the most problems finding work. Employers are encouraged to hire high school students who traditionally have the most trouble in finding summer jobs.
Challenge offers five options to employers, students and young people. SEED, the Summer Employment Experience Development option, provides wage subsidies to employers to create summer jobs for students. As far as possible, SEED complements provincial and territorial student employment programs, a co-operative process started under this government in 1985.

Last month, I announced that $88 million will be spent on the Summer Employment Experience Development component of Challenge '93. That is an increase of $5.1 million over the amount set aside last year for SEED.
I also decided to extend for one week, until March 19-tomorrow-the deadline for applying under SEED. By extending the deadline and increasing funding, we want to encourage employers in the private sector to create as many summer jobs as possible this year.
We believe employers realize that by creating summer jobs for students, they are helping Canada's labour force of the future. Despite the prevailing economic climate, students should not give up on finding a job.
We also increased funding for the Student Business Loan Program, from $0.9 million to $1.14 million.
The purpose of the Student Business Loan Program is to help young people who would like to start a business to create their own summer jobs. Under the program, students can get loans of up to $3,000 to operate their own small business during the summer.
In 1985, first year of the program 101 loans were approved and 229 summer jobs were created. In 1992, the number of loans approved was 995 and as a result 2,218 students were able to find summer jobs.
This component is offered through the Federal Business Development Bank, in co-operation with the Royal Bank of Canada and the National Bank of Canada.
This year British Columbia will join the group of provinces that offer this component of the Challenge
Supply
Program: Newfoundland, Quebec, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the two territories.

The business drive for jobs is a collaborative effort by business organizations and companies to challenge their members and the business community to create additional employment for students during the summer without using government wage subsidies.
With its local hiring emphasis the business drive for jobs helps both students and employers. Students gain work experience and learn about career opportunities in local businesses. By the same token, the employers are introduced to potential future employees.
Another challenge option is the Native Internship Program which creates employment opportunities within Employment and Immigration Canada offices for aboriginal students. It is designed to enhance the job search skills of participants and to introduce them to public service as a possible career.
Another of EIC's youth initiatives is the co-operative education program which channels funds to educational institutions to assist them in running provincially approved work-study programs.
Last August I announced almost $25 million in new funding for co-operative education for the period 1992-96. This is an increase of about $4.5 million over the 1991-95 allocation. It will go toward co-operative education programs at 135 secondary and post-secondary institutions across Canada.
As I said at the time, co-operative education plays a significant role in helping young people gain valuable work-related experience. It is an important bridge between the classroom and the labour market.
Altogether, EIC programs specifically for young people, including stay in school, co-operative education and SEED, spent over $211 million nationally in 1992-93 helping young people find temporaiy employment and preparing them for full-time participation in the labour force. This is on top of our regular employment and training programs that are also widely used by young people.

Supply

We are accused of not keeping our commitments to the young people of this country. I disagree. We also have agreements with Newfoundland and New Brunswick concerning the Youth Strategy. These agreements were first signed in 1988 to help young people in these provinces continue their education and get the training and experience they need.
Perhaps the hon. member would care to explain to 17,600 young people in New Brunswick who took advantage of services provided by access centres financed jointly by the federal and provincial governments in what way this government has failed to meet its commitments. These centres offer young people counselling and evaluation services and direct them to training, study and job creation programs offered by the federal and provincial governments. Most of the young people who come to the access centres are between 15 and 24 years old. About 45 per cent dropped out of high school very early on and need basic training.
When we asked young people whether they had a place to go to talk about jobs, training, education or personal problems before the access centres were created, 64 per cent of the young men and 71 per cent of the young women replied they did not. When asked whether they were satisfied with the help they received at the centres, 86 per cent of the young men and 90 per cent of the young women said they were satisfied or very satisfied.

I suggest the hon. member talk to these Canadians.
Federal and provincial contributions for the Newfoundland agreement total $56.5 million of which $39.5 million represents federal contributions. As of late 1992 there were approximately 2,200 participants actively involved in Youth Strategy projects in Newfoundland. A total of 9,500 youth had participated directly in projects sponsored under the Youth Strategies since 1988-89 and another estimated 50,000 youth have been directly affected by these projects.
These are just a few of the ongoing efforts by this government to help Canada's young people. Rather than "robbing" young Canadians as the motion alleges, this
government has moved to do precisely what needs to be done.
Of course we need a competent and highly qualified labour force. Of course the government is concerned about the problems facing young Canadians on the labour market.
What will the future be? There will be stimulating opportunities, but also certain realities that will be more difficult to cope with. Young Canadians can choose from a range of more than 15,000 occupations and a wealth of innovative courses that will help them acquire the knowledge and skills they need.
On the other hand, the labour market is becoming increasingly complex. Because of global competition and new technologies, Canada's labour force of the future will have to meet tougher standards. Today's youth will have to stay in school longer and have more skills than past generations. To be competitive students must have a solid grounding in mathematics, languages and science.
As I just explained, we are doing what has to be done to help the young people of this country prepare for the challenges of a constantly changing world. We are certain that our young people and the entire country will be able to meet these challenges.

Mr. Speaker, the minister spoke about problems of financing. The government has found $5.8 billion for helicopters which chase submarines. Does he know that if that money were spent on things like youth programs, I am told there would be up to 75 times more jobs created. That is if the money were spent that way rather than on submarinechasing helicopters.

I must say to the minister that I fully support this program, which is intended to help people continue their education. But can he quote any figures to indicate the level of funding for this program? Does the program have any funds left, and which regions will be able to take advantage of this funding? Apparently there is a lack of funding in some of Canada's regions.
March 18, 1993

Finally, I also have a question about the school dropout rate. I will quote what was said in Agenda for Youth, a report by the Liberal Senate and House Committee on Youth, published three months ago. It indicates, for instance, the partial illiteracy rate among individuals between the ages of 16 and 34 and born in Canada. Among young people between the ages of 16 and 24, the illiteracy rate is almost 30 per cent, while innumeracy is almost 45 per cent. Among 25-year-olds the illiteracy rate is nearly 20 per cent, while innumeracy is about 30 per cent.
What do the minister and the government opposite intend to do in this rapidly changing world, to deal with this effectively-and I am not talking about what they said they would do, because it is easy to say a lot of nice words that don't mean much-what will they actually do to help young people across Canada?

Mr. Speaker, in concluding the hon. member said that nice words are not enough. That is quite true. We are accustomed to hearing that sort of thing from hon. members opposite, words that fail to offer any solution whatever. For instance, the Official Opposition wants to get rid of the GST but they will not tell us now what alternative they have in mind and how much it will cost Canadian taxpayers.
That being said, I agree with my hon. friend that words are not enough, and it' he had listened to all 20 minutes of my speech in which I mentioned some of the practical steps that have been taken by the Government of Canada to help the young people of this country he probably would not have put his question. But he did, which again goes to show that to them what you say is more important than what you do, although they would never admit it.
Again, I regret the fact that my hon. friend, and I assume this is part of their strategy, tried to compare the helicopter program-because that is what he was referring to-to other programs in other envelopes of this government. I may remind him that although these are hard times, the government invested-and I am getting back to his second question-$296 million in the Stay in School Program to deal with a very serious problem. I don't think we should play politics with the high school dropout rate in this country, since these young people are tomorrow's labour force and some of them will take our seats in this House.
We must do something about this fundamental problem. Education will provide the necessary tools to meet
Supply
the challenges of the future in a rapidly changing world, a global economy, and a world of fierce competition. We must concentrate our efforts on dealing with this problem. The hon. member would have Canadians believe that the Challenge budget was cut in half, but he is wrong, Mr. Speaker, There was some redeployment of funding within the program in order to focus on the fundamental problem: the school dropout rate. However, the other initiatives and options in the program are there to deal with other problems. Yes, funding is still available. This is a five-year program, and we allocate funding by region, as we have done since the beginning of the program.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the minister. He has laid out for us some of the initiatives the government has taken. I am somewhat surprised he did not mention the fact that in the late seventies and early eighties when the Liberals formed the government they began the process of cutting back on transfers to the provinces. They began the process of capping the transfers.
Research we have done into this seems to indicate that the major provinces, those that are seen to be healthy, had the biggest change in funding. In the province of Ontario that amounts to something like $4.4 billion in different types of funding that has been removed from the province's budget.
I am surprised that the minister did not at least acknowledge that the Liberal government began this process. It is true that his government has embellished it, but when one makes a major structural financial change such as that in how schools are funded, how can one possibly be suqmsed and shocked that the drop-out rates have escalated, that illiteracy continues to flourish and that children still live in poverty? When one initiates a major fiscal change such as the Liberals did the end result of that surely is obvious. All of the resultant problems are right there in our educational system today.
I am somewhat surprised that the minister did not even give credit where the credit is due, to the Liberal Party of Canada.

However, I absolutely do not want to deal with that specific issue. I will leave that to hon. members to debate among themselves.

Mr. Speaker, I will make my question short.
The problem we have is that the minister gets up and talks about all the programs the government has been responsible for initiating, all the statistics and all the numbers. The problem is that there is a difference between what is happening in the programs and what is going on in reality.
I am convinced that the lack of action on these programs is something that many members of Parliament are not focusing on. There are a lot of good programs in the Government of Canada and some of them go back many years. They are not just Conservative programs, a lot of good programs are Liberal programs. But we are having a problem today actioning these programs.
We have these kids out on the street who hear about the Challenge program or the retraining programs but when they go to either fill out the forms or try to get involved in one of them they come back empty. What they are asking is: "What good are all these programs"?
It is not unlike the Small Businesses Loans Act. I have been made to look almost like a fool in the last two weeks by the government promoting the Small Businesses Loans Act. It sends the small businessmen to the local banks and they come back not knowing anything about it because the government has not actioned its own policy.
I wonder if the minister would care to react to that and maybe in the spirit of non-partisanship admit that even though there are some good programs in the hopper, they are not being implemented fully.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend raises a few interesting points. Some of them I am prepared to acknowledge. It is true that some of the programs in place right now were in place before this government
came to office. Because those few we kept were good, we have enhanced them and maintained them. I am prepared to admit that.
We have also brought in the other programs that go hand in hand with those in order to give the greatest number of opportunities to our young people.
When my friend suggests that there are some programs that are either misunderstood or perhaps even not applied, that is probably true. In some cases it is because programs have been changed or are in the process of being changed. Perhaps some people, rightly or wrongly, did not get the appropriate information at the right time to respond to the people to whom my friend is referring. That of course has to be corrected.
There is absolutely no question that if the programs need to be enhanced or corrected this minister is prepared to look at that very seriously. In fact, the prosperity initiative is going to permit us to do more in order to make sure that all of our initiatives address the entire picture, not just piece by piece. Sometimes the puzzle does not fit.
I think we all agree that we need the appropriate education, the appropriate training programs, the appropriate initiatives and also the connection between all this, particularly to address the step between school, college, university and the labour force. This has to be ironed out and the prosperity initiatives address that. The means and needs are going to be put in place in order to make sure that the system works and works properly.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have this opportunity once more to participate in a debate on policies which are designed to provide young people with some answers to some of the serious problems of employment and social and economic dislocation that they face these days.
I suppose the point at which to begin this debate is to refer to the year 1985. That year was declared by the United Nations to be International Youth Year. I led a New Democratic task force on youth that went across the country talking to young people that year. They were given an opportunity to express their views on what their concerns were at the time and what the solutions might be.
March 18, 1993

.(1115)
It should be understood that one of the concerns within the United Nations was that in the industrial nations of the world there were accumulating large numbers of unemployed youth, youth who not only did not have jobs but who had very little prospect of jobs. There was concern that not having jobs would ultimately lead to a group within society that would constitute a serious social problem.
At that time, the government also sponsored a number of youth fora across the country within the context of International Youth Year. A number of us in this House attempted to get the government to introduce a coherent youth policy. We just heard the minister say that the prosperity initiative was somehow going to address the issue of a coherent youth policy. That just demonstrates one thing: that the government at the time, having made the promise it would adopt a youth policy that would address the issue of youth unemployment, failed to meet its promise. Now in 1993 we have yet another promise that will address the issue. There could be no clearer, more dramatic demonstration of the failure of this government's policies with respect to youth.
The report provided by Stats Canada in January entitled "Labour Market Trends for Youth 1989 to 1992" is interesting because it corresponds to the introduction of the free trade agreement as well as the beginning of the recession, really a depression, that exist now.
No matter what the minister may have said about the immediate short-term gains in youth employment, the fact is that between 1989 and 1992 youth unemployment rose from 11 per cent to 19.3 per cent. Unemployment among youth grew from 303,000 in 1989 to 431,000 in 1992, beginning to mimic the situation in the years 1984 and 1985.
What I think is significant in all of this is not only that youth unemployment has increased, but the number of youth who are looking for jobs, that is the number of youth in the labour force, has dropped. This is an expression of the hopelessness that plagues youth these days, that same kind of hopelessness which was identified back in 1984 and 1985.
We can refer to another bit of information which has been given broad public debate and discussion in recent
Supply
months and that is the appearance of generation x. It is the product, the predicted product, of the failure of the governments of the eighties, including this government, in 1984, 1985 and continuing to this day. Unless something dramatic is done we may face yet another kind of generation, perhaps generation omega, those who are completely through and those who are completely disillusioned, disenfranchised and disempowered and consider themselves outside the pale.
The fact is that we have a serious unemployment rate. We have a serious problem with respect to the ability of young people to adapt to the new knowledge-based economy we now face.
We identified dramatic changes in 1985 in our task force report which have to be addressed. Youth must be prepared, but those initiatives simply have not taken place.
It is interesting to recall that just a few days ago the House justice committee published a report in which it indicated that if one really wants to address the issue of crime prevention in Canada, one has to focus increasingly on young people at risk and the underlying social economic factors associated with crime and criminality.
Certainly, if we are going to address crime then we have to address its roots. Crime is one of the expressions of the disillusionment and disenfranchisement of young people. Since 1984, the year before International Youth Year, there has been a 405 per cent increase in violent crime committed by youth. In general it would be too simple to describe it in these terms, but at least in part it is an expression of the frustration that inevitably will come to young people who are looking for jobs in the absence of any coherent policy to provide them with jobs and the training for those jobs in a population that has a 30 per cent innumeracy and illiteracy rate, which is an issue that has not been adequately addressed.
It has to be admitted that the illiteracy rate among youth is no higher than the general population, but in this day and age one would expect the educational system to provide better preparation than that. There is a 35 per cent drop-out rate in our school system. That reflects some of the concerns we heard when we had our task force. Youth thought their schools served them poorly. For example, we found, insofar as vocational

March 18, 1993
Supply
counselling was concerned, that the average high school student in this country faces a situation in which there is one counsellor for each 1,000 or 2,000 students. They need more help in that regard. They also said they wanted more co-operative programs and more work experience programs associated with schooling at the high school level.
There were a number of things that we suggested should be done at the time. Among those was to increase the funding available for co-operative and work experience programs. More important, we suggested a number of approaches to improve the situation with respect to training and education for youth. I will come to these in a moment.
We heard the minister bragging about the tremendous initiatives this government has undertaken. I have already indicated that this government's youth policies have been a failure. One might wonder why, in view of the large number and diversity of programs cited by the ministers, they are nevertheless inadequate. Well, they seem to have multiplied in a very peculiar way; they have increased in number but decreased in size.
We heard the minister, and it bothered me immensely, brag about the youth employment centres. The youth employment centres on college campuses right across this country have been closed down. We heard him talk about the Canadian Jobs Strategy and what contributions it was making to youth training and retraining. The fact is that while the Canadian Jobs Strategy, to an extent of 40 per cent, serves youth the government has cut $200 million from that program. It multiplied the programs and decreased the resources.
We heard the minister talk about the SEED program and the Challenge program. This is one area where we must concede to the Liberals. When this government came into office it cut the amount of money available for student summer employment from $240 million ultimately to $180 million right now.
We heard him talk about the SEED program. We heard him talk about co-operative programs. In order to fund work experience or co-operative programs for high school students the government took money from the
SEED program and shifted it over to the high school level, resulting in $140 million being cut to $80 million for the SEED program. We heard the minister say that the SEED program has been increased from $80 million to $88 million over the last four years. While all that was going on the unemployment rate has almost doubled for young people, particularly in the summer.
That is hardly a record to stand before this House and brag about. We have heard my colleague mention what the government has done with respect to its obligations for post-secondary education. The accumulated cuts to the university and college system as a result of this government's actions, as well as those of the Liberal government before it, will amount to about $10 billion in a decade.
What is the result of that? The result is that universities find themselves severely cash-strapped. Libraries are in a state of deterioration. Laboratories are using archaic microscopes. I dare say that if the present trend continues the microscope of Antoni van Leeuwenhoek will be used in some of the laboratories of this country.
Not only are students gaining access to a university and a college system that cannot do a good job of preparing students for a new technological future, but to get there it costs more. Tuition fees have increased right across this country. I will give some examples. Between 1985-86 and 1991-1992 tuition for engineering undergraduates increased 145 per cent at McGill, 82 per cent at the University of Saskatchewan, and 92 per cent at Simon Fraser.
Meanwhile, because of these increased tuition costs
70,000	students were turned away from the universities and colleges of this nation last year.
This government's policies, which are intended to encourage university graduation and encourage students to gain an education, have resulted in a situation as a result of the real actions of this government in which on many campuses there are food banks. There are food banks at the University of Toronto, Simon Fraser University, the University of Manitoba, the University of Alberta and Dalhousie University.
March 18, 1993

Where do students from ordinary families get the funding to go to university or college? They get it from the Canada Student Loans Program. What is happening to that? This government is in the process of making it worse and worse. Just recently Bill C-76 passed through this House. Let me just mention something about Bill C-76 and the promises the government made back in 1985 about consultation and concern about youth. That bill went to a legislative committee which refused to hear from students, refused to hear what students would say about the fact that this government had imposed a 3 per cent tax on student loans and then turned around and eliminated the six-month interest-free period.
The government tried to make it sound good by promising those same students that the 3 per cent tax on student loans, which means that a student goes in and borrows a couple of thousand dollars and before he can get it home must pay $60 out of his pocket right then and there, would be eliminated when it eliminated the interest-free period. It did not do that.
Students have had the government stick its hands in their pockets for a total of about $70 million in additional costs to students across this country for a program which is supposed to encourage accessibility to universities.
Now it intends to make it a single bank program in which student loans would be made available on the same basis as any other private loan, a single bank perhaps will do it. It is going to insist that a student carry at least 80 per cent of a full load thus making it more and more difficult for part-time students to gain access to university. This government has a lot of nerve coming into this House and bragging about what it has done for young people, who are hurting right across this country.
We urgently need a coherent, broadly-based program to eliminate illiteracy among youth, to ensure that every child in this country, as our party suggests, will have access in this new socio-economic environment to the necessary preparation for school through a broadly-based increase in the availability of day care, not day care for just care but day care for education.

We need a program that will provide broader access to work experience such as the national community youth service that we suggested. We need a program that will provide funding, as we suggested in our task force report, for youth between the ages of 18 and 24 for two years to make it possible for them to go to college or university, to engage in entrepreneurship, to be retrained or to take apprenticeship for two years. That would ensure that more and more of our youth would have access to a reasonable choice about what kind of training or educational alternatives, and therefore vocations, are suitable to them and it would not be dictated by their ability to pay. These are the kinds of programs we need.
Mr. Speaker, if you want to see a government that is interested in youth then contrast the cutbacks by this federal government to the 70 per cent increase in youth training funds in Ontario, to the JOY program of last summer which appealed to so many young people.
I want to congratulate the Liberals for having introduced this motion. I want to congratulate them for having had a report on the needs of youth. That report was an excellent report in reporting the needs but it was very short on describing the solutions. They are calling the kettle black when they accuse this government of not having policies. They came late to the scene.
I hope in identifying the problems as the Liberals have in that report and in condemning the government for what it has done that they will do in this area what they have not done in very many areas, and that is come up with policies that will address the issues they have raised in more specific terms than they seem inclined to do.

They both are members of the same political party. I would like him to comment on some of the actions taken by Mr. Rae with regard to students.
The member knows that education is primarily a provincial responsibility. As I understand it, his friend and colleague, Mr. Rae, the premier of Ontario, has cut

back on funding for students wishing to attend post-secondary institutions. That is the first part of my question.

However, the NDP are quick to suggest new programs but very rarely does it attach a price tag to any of these specific programs.
