Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has perhaps been in this House when I have expressed deep concern about the action by the Ontario government in eliminating grants to students. However, it should be understood that the grants to students were coming out of provincial coffers. When we really look at it, that was one way of shifting the cost to the Canada Student Loans Program and therefore increasing the available provincial funding to universities.
This is a direct result of the cuts in EPF initiated by the Liberal governments beginning in 1975. Yet I would say the new super-minister of education and training, my colleague Dave Cooke in Windsor, agrees with me. I have no doubt a re-examination will take place with respect to that.
In respect to some of the programs I have suggested, I suppose there would be some curiosity among the Liberals about the ideas that the New Democrats have brought forward. The Liberals will inevitably see what they can borrow. That is why their youth report contains so little substance. We will be specific about those programs I have suggested.
In fact the child care program we have suggested will cost $100 million in the first year and ultimately $1.7 million in the last year. This is within the context of a broadly-based program of worker empowerment training and education and investment. After five years it will ultimately lead to a $10 billion cut in the deficit.
With respect to the program I have advocated concerning youth prospects which would provide two years of training to young people between the ages of 18 and 24, this was costed. In the first year it would cost about $400 million and ultimately about $1 billion. That of course does not take into account the expenditures already being made with respect to the administration of other student aid programs which would incur a savings if this kind of program were introduced.

Mr. Speaker, my friend raced through those numbers so quickly he hardly had time to breathe. He talked about a $10 billion return. Is he really serious about that with regard to the first program he was mentioning? Where does he propose to get the money from? In the second program he talked about $400 million. He said it so quickly it almost sounded more like four cents or 40 cents. That is a lot of cabbage. I am sure that my friend will agree.
Where does he propose that money will come from? He knows as we speak that his friend Roy Romanow is about to cut the civil service in the province of Saskatchewan. He is about to cut loose all his friends in the labour movement. Bob Rae as we speak is talking about cutting back tens of thousands of civil servants in the province of Ontario.
While they are talking about cutting back at the provincial level, they have their youth critic here in Ottawa talking about spending, spending, spending, in a very irresponsible fashion I would submit. I would hope that the hon. member and his party, before they start talking about all these new programs, would be kind enough to inform us in detail where this money is to come from.
Rather than simply saying that we give it time and as the economy improves we will end up paying for it, someone has to pay the bill every month. It seems that members of the NDP are always inclined not to worry about the fact that there is a mortgage payment or a rental payment coming up at the end of the month; they are just prepared to put this country and this province further into debt.
Is it any wonder they have so very little credibility?

Mr. Speaker, I do not know how this hon. member has the gall to stand up here and talk about
March 18, 1993

credibility. He has already demonstrated to the whole nation watching this debate on television that he is an extremely slow thinker, even for a member of the right wing of the Liberal Party.
I know I might have gone too fast for the hon. member. I think it is important for him to understand that we are talking about a federal issue here and the role of the federal government.
We are not going to talk about the cutbacks. We are not going to talk about the cutbacks in the civil service by a Liberal government in Newfoundland or a Liberal government in New Brunswick or a Liberal government in Quebec. We are not going to talk about the fact that those Liberal governments have higher proportional and faster growing deficits than Ontario.
We are not going to talk about that, but I will continue to go as slowly as I can so that this right wing deficit preoccupied member of the Liberal Party who seems to be so slow in grasping things will understand.
I did not say, for example, that day care all by itself would lead to a $10 billion cut in the deficit. What I said was that an over-all program designed to produce jobs of the sort that the Liberals have been challenged by almost every newspaper in this country to produce and will not, will lead to in context over all a $10 billion cut in the deficit over five years.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member's time has expired. I am sure he will be able to read it in Hansard.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to address the House on this motion as proposed by my good friend the hon. member for Haldimand-Norfolk. It is a fact that young Canadians are confronted by numerous challenges. Steps we take to help them will have a direct impact on all our lives.
Last year I had the privilege of serving as co-chair of the Liberal Senate and House of Commons committee on youth. My colleagues and I travelled across Canada. We went to every province and the Arctic and met with hundreds of Canadians, both young people and those interested in helping them.
We met with teachers, students, fishermen, farmers, police officers, people who run drop-in centres as well as
Supply
aboriginal groups and multicultural groups. Through those meetings we learned a great deal about the state of youth in Canada. I can say that for many of them the situation is bleak.
Young people today are faced by rising unemployment, fears about job security and feelings of alienation. They are frustrated by an education system that cannot help the 100,000 high school students who lose hope and drop out of high school every year. That is 100,000 a year, one million in a decade. It is a system that fails to address the high illiteracy and high innumeracy rates that afflict our youth.
Young people worry about not having the skills needed to find jobs in tomorrow's knowledge-based economy. They cannot understand why the federal government will not provide them with opportunities.
Everywhere our youth committee went, whether it was in Moncton, Quebec City or in Edmonton, the message was always the same: Young Canadians feel that they have no future. Many are deeply troubled by the present situation. They are desperate for a new vision of Canada, a vision that will restore their hope and show them a future.
Young people, their parents, their teachers, people in youth-serving organizations all look to the government for guidance and leadership. Sadly, this government has turned a deaf ear to their concerns.
For the past two years our youth have struggled alongside other Canadians through the worst recession in recent memory while the government turns its back on the human misery created by the recession. Is there misery in this country? Ask the two million Canadians lining up at food banks. Forty per cent of that number are under the age of 18.
That neglectful attitude is also evident in other areas. Look at the unemployment rate. While the general population now has a rate of 10.8 per cent, youth unemployment stands at 16.7 per cent which means that almost 400,000 young people are listed as unemployed. That is a trend which has maintained itself throughout the recession.
The youth unemployment rate has always stood at approximately six percentage points higher than the general unemployment rate. The number of unemployed youth has risen steadily since 1988, going from 303,000 to
431,000	in 1992.

March 18, 1993
Supply
How did this Progressive Conservative government respond? Well, it responded by diminishing opportunities for young people. Because of government cuts the jobs created by SEED, the summer job creation program, went from 94,115 in 1985 to 53,800 in 1991.
The government has also cut deeply into funding for post-secondary education and in training programs for youth. In 1991 the Conservative government cut transfers for education by almost a half billion dollars and in the 1992 budget another $800 million was cut.
This assault on youth has to stop. A new generation of political leadership in this country will achieve that.
I was born in 1960. My generation grew up believing that if we worked hard and received a good education we could expect to do better than our parents did. But as we see, times have changed and that is no longer the case.
As a member of Parliament I have spent the past four years listening to the voices of young people throughout Canada. I can say that an entire generation of young Canadians is learning that the rules for inclusion in our society have changed. Instead of an unlimited future, today's youth are confronted by diminishing opportunities.
The Liberal Party of Canada is determined to restore hope and offer a future to Canada's youth. We are determined to get our economy moving again, rebuild Canada's economic leadership, create highly skilled, highly paid jobs and reclaim the future for our children. We want to create a society that will be able to compete globally, protect the environment and provide opportunities for its members.
Young people are an important part of our vision. That is why we are committed to giving them the tools they need to build their future in the new economy, an economy where young people will be full partners.
We call on all our economic partners-business, labour, all levels of government-to join us in a program to eradicate illiteracy and innumeracy among our youth. We call on them to help us promote co-operative education, to encourage work place training and to help us develop national education strategy goals.
The Liberal Party of Canada is committed to establishing a national apprenticeship training program, to creating a Canadian youth service dedicated to environmental protection and responding to the social needs of our communities.
The Chretien plan outlined earlier this year offers the promise of developing an educated work force with world-class skills. It offers the promise of a globally competitive economy and a learning culture that can easily adapt to change.
This is the direction in which we want to go. This is the Liberal vision of the future. We are determined to make that vision a reality.
The message we have received from young people is clear: They do not want political leaders to sit idly by; they want them to act. Government has a moral responsibility to provide opportunities for its young people. In turn, young people have a moral responsibility to make the most out of those opportunities.
Young people understand they have an important role to play and they are ready to take up that challenge. They also understand that the future is not a gift, it is an accomplishment.
We know on this side of the House that by building an effective partnership with the key stakeholders and young Canadians we can achieve the vision that we have outlined today.
The future of this country depends largely on the political will to act and to effect positive change for young generations. For far too long, this government has been silent on developing an effective agenda for young people.
I think that we, as an opposition party in Parliament, have outlined to the government what we as a party in government would do. It is a serious program that I am sure will make a difference. Together with young people we will make it happen.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to compliment the member for York North on an excellent address that outlines a direction and a policy. I think that all members should be cognizant that this particular member has done a lot of work with respect to youth and the agenda for youth.
March 18, 1993

I know that in the process of preparing for the new direction that the Liberal Party is going to offer with respect to youth the member for York North travelled around the country and consulted. Therefore the recommendations and the views that are expressed have come from the bottom up rather than from the dictatorial methods employed by the government.
I wondered whether the member could tell us of his visit to Atlantic Canada. I know he was in my own riding of Moncton. What feedback was the member getting from youth and what directions did they indicate that we as a government should take?

I would first like to stress the point made by the hon. member that I think is of extreme importance. We as Liberals realized a long time ago that there must be a new style of politics in the 1990s and that people must be partners in the development of policy with our party and indeed within our country.
I may tell you that 3 of these 10 recommendations that are part of the agenda for youth are now a part of our electoral platform. Unlike what the members opposite often say about opposition parties that do not make their agendas available early on, I can sincerely say that we have been telling the Conservative government since January what our agenda for youth will be.
On the point raised about Atlantic Canada, there is a generation of young Canadians in Atlantic Canada who reflect the national concerns. They have fears about job security. They are concerned about the unemployment rate. They are concerned about how the federal government has not been able to equip them with the vehicles of opportunity to deal with global changes, the global economy and global competitiveness.
What is of major concern to Atlantic youth is also that their economy is being restructured but nothing is being done-not only for them but for their parents-during this adjustment period. They feel shut out and alienated from the entire process of government.
The Liberal Party, as the modern party that it is today, has decided to open the doors wide to ask Canadians at the grass roots level to tell us what they think and what their concerns are. I am proud to say that the agenda for youth is not only the work of parliamentarians but it is the work of young people from the Atlantic to the
Supply
Pacific, from coast to coast to coast. That is the way this party will proceed for many years to come.

Mr. Speaker, I would first of all like to commend my colleague from Haldimand-Norfolk for this opposition motion because I believe that the subject is extremely important. I would also like to commend the member for York North for co-chairing the committee which studied the problems of youth throughout Canada. I believe that these two events will hopefully make a tremendous contribution to this great challenge facing the country today. For me, the fundamental question today is this: What should we do, what do our young people need today?

Let us look at that. It seems to me that what Canadians want-young people in particular-is hope, empowerment, dignity and an education that will lead to jobs. Clearly that has to be the focus of government because our future, yours and mine, Mr. Speaker, depends upon our young people being well educated and well trained and having the kinds of jobs that can not only sustain that which we have in our country today but also that which can be used to build upon for future generations.
The recession is supposedly over and yet we are talking about unemployment rates of 16 per cent and 17 per cent. In some parts of the country for our young people it is in excess of 20 per cent. If we were to go to certain groups in our society, for example our aboriginal people, it would be very, very close to total unemployment. This is a far cry from full employment.
That depresses me. I take it that that concern is shared by all my fellow parliamentarians.
I remember travelling across Canada a couple of years ago to talk to the young people in our colleges and universities and other young people who were in the work force to ask them about how they saw the country and their future. There was uncertainty. There was not the enthusiasm that one normally sees among our young people. I noted and they reminded me that both education and jobs are rapidly escaping the grasp of many of our young people today.

Supply
Between 1985-86 and 1992-93, tuition fees have skyrocketed out of sight. Let me give some examples. The fees have grown by 69 per cent at Memorial University and 185.7 per cent at Northwest Community College in British Columbia. I could give more examples that are even more striking.
Those are tuition fees. We often forget to talk about incidental fees, which are those other fees that students need to pay. They have grown in certain sectors by even greater percentages.
For the first time in our history the young people of Canada are paying the goods and services tax on books and reading materials so they are being hit again. They are unable to find suitable employment. The summer of 1992 was one of the worst ever for young people. They either had no jobs or if they did have jobs they were poorly remunerated short-term jobs so they were unable to save and contribute as fully as they could have to their education this year. It was a real disaster. I am really hoping, as I know my colleagues are, that things will really change.
What has been the government's record with respect to post-secondary education and making it more accessible? Without being partisan whatsoever I assure you that it has not at all been laudable. I will let the people be the judge.
Let me share this with you. The criteria for the allocation of student loans was set in 1984, almost a decade ago. What has changed? Absolutely nothing. This is totally inadequate. Obviously the costs have gone up dramatically. I will give an example of someone who is going into the faculty of dentistry in my province. The loan money that he or she can get will not even cover the fees for that particular student. Surely that is inadequate. Surely we are reaching the level where education becomes available to those who are the richest in society.
Quite apart from not changing the student aid program in a positive kind of way, the government did some very regressive things. It imposed a 3 per cent tax on student loans Mr. Speaker, if you, and I had to borrow as students it was because we did not have enough money. Obviously that is why we borrow. Yet at the same time it has imposed a 3 per cent tax on that. Those who do not
have to borrow do not have to pay the tax. However, those who do not have the resources have to pay the tax.
What else did it do? There used to be a six-month interest-free period so that I, as a student, could graduate, get a job and then start repaying my loan. What has happened? Now it is in the process of changing that. There is going to be six months' interest more to pay. It is interesting that the 3 per cent tax is going to yield to the government coffers, according to government estimates, $22.5 million. This additional six months' interest would yield to the government coffers, once it is fully instituted, $35 million. That is an additional almost $60 million out of the pockets of our young people.
That is what the government has done.
What has happened as a result of that? Obviously student debt has gone up at an exponential rate. It is really going out of sight.
I want to share the following example with you, Mr. Speaker, because I know how interested you are in young people. There has been a 500 per cent increase in the number of students who graduate with a total debt burden in excess of $10,000 during the last four years.
Now the government is talking about the first step toward privatizing the student aid program. It sends out submissions to banks to ask them if they could handle it. The students are very clever. They say: "Just a minute, there".

What criteria will guide the decisions in making student loans? Then they asked who will set these criteria and what the role of the bank or banks will be in this whole process.
Mr. Speaker, I assure you that students are very nervous. Why? Of course if they have money there is not so much of a problem. However, if they have few resources what will happen? Will colleges and universities be less accessible? Will these young men and women who want to pursue their education be able to do so with a loan that they will have to repay later?
March 18, 1993



I want to recap and point out that the government has cut transfer payments to the provinces for post-secondary education. I have said it time and time again in this House. In roughly a decade of government control it will have reduced and cut back the grants and the transfer payments for health and education by $30 billion. It is not $30 million but $30 billion. It is about $20 billion for health and about $10 billion for education.
As a result, as I indicated, the universities have increased their tuitions and incidental fees. Student loan criteria have not changed since 1984. There have been some regressive measures such as the 3 per cent tax and the addition of six months' interest. All of that, quite apart from the goods and services tax, is penalizing students. They have taken hit after hit after hit with no relief.
These students are graduating with huge debt loads and the prospects of a job are not particularly good; they are either over the short term, poorly remunerated or they do not exist.
Let me share some examples as to how the student aid program, quite apart from the 3 per cent tax and the additional six months' interest, has really caused difficulty-
There is a young woman in my riding-and I could give a dozen such examples of this-she is the mother of three. She defaulted on her student loan because she was unable to find a suitable job. She was unable to find any job. Now she is being threatened with the possible seizure of her child tax credit on her income tax return. She really is. This is the absolute truth. Besides that, she is being harassed by a collection agency.
I understand that one has to try to collect the money but one cannot draw blood from a stone. Surely a mother of three who has done her best to get a job should not be harassed by anyone for money that she cannot repay.
In another instance, I have a constituent who took out a student loan and decided to take a three-year program at university. He studied for two years, ran out of money and went back to work in a responsible kind of way. He then wanted to go back and complete the third year. Lo and behold, that was not possible because he had supposedly defaulted on his loan.
Supply
Now he has to wait. Will he be able to borrow money again? After he has gone through a number of hoops and hurdles, I suspect that it will be possible.
Can one agree with me that this is not the kind of program that we need? This is not the kind of program that you and I and other parliamentarians want. We need a program that is going to be truly sensitive to the needs of young people and will encourage them to finish their education.
I know I am running out of time. I do wish I had another hour. I am sure that I could share some insights that would be useful not only to my parliamentary colleagues but as well to Canadians. I am sure some members of government will disagree with me, but let me say that even our training efforts are not particularly appropriate.
Many jobs are available today and yet training is unavailable to respond to those jobs. I am delighted that the leader of the Liberal Party has started to make very important statements about where the party stands with respect to education, on the job training, a Canada youth service, and our commitment to education. He issued a statement saying we want the best education training and retraining programs in the whole world so we can be competitive.
We need to make education accessible. We need to improve training and retraining to make apprenticeship and vocational training as well as a whole gamut of educational programs available if we want this nation to be a leader among nations and our young people to be leaders rather than followers.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my hon. friend for his comments on education.
As he knows from travelling across the country, as he did from university to university talking to post-secondary education students, there really is a feeling out there of despair. We have a whole group of students coming out of university with no hope of a job.
As was seen in the The Globe and Mail this morning, the article headed, "Escaping the Student Debt Trap", we have hundreds and hundreds of examples of how students are going through university piling up debt upon debt. A student piled up $20,000 in government loans.

March 18, 1993
Supply
He then got out of university and had no chance of paying those debts back because he could not get a job.
I know the hon. member has talked to thousands of students across the country. He brought out a great report on ways he feels universities and governments can better adapt to these changing times in order to help students not only to get jobs but to get the education they need to find these jobs in order for Canada to compete internationally.
I want to ask my hon. friend where does he feel the government should be putting its priorities today in terms of education? Given that we have limited resources and that when the books finally come out in the next budget it is going to show that our national finances are in extremely rough shape, where should we be putting the priorities in terms of education?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for the question.
He indicated was there were three reports that were a result of travelling across the country and consulting with young Canadians over the last three years. They are available and I would be delighted to share them. They are non-partisan documents. They simply identify the issues, concerns and challenges.
With respect to where priorities ought to be placed, I think we should listen very carefully to young people, for example the Canadian Federation of Students. I presented a petition today on behalf of students from Saskatchewan. They represent over 450,000 students. They and the community colleges are telling us the following:
We understand we are in very difficult financial times. We are willing to do our part, but we also have to ensure we do not save money today and sacrifice tomorrow. We have to ensure not only that there is adequate money for education, training, retraining, literacy programs, research and development, but that the money is spent in the best way possible to respond to Canada's challenges.
What are those challenges? We all agree that economic development, the creation of jobs for young people, those who need jobs has to be the first priority. We also recognize, and I have said this through petitions and oral questions, that one of the greatest challenges this country faces-quite apart from economic development, the creation of good, long-term, well-remunerated jobs-are our social challenges. Look at the poor today. There are five million Canadians living at or below the
level of poverty, most of whom are women, over one million who are children. Over two million Canadians will be fed at food banks. Over two million Canadians will receive social assistance.
These groups are often powerless. They do not have the necessary skills and education to integrate fully into society. We have to target moneys to those particular groups to make sure that they can, by themselves, have that which they need in order to get jobs and contribute fully to society.
We have to recognize that when they are not doing that they need to collect assistance from the public purse, and when they do that they do not feel very good about it. They want to be contributing to the public purse. That is what I would do, absolutely.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel R. Tremblay (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will comment on the dynamic leading role which the Department of the Secretary of State plays in helping our young people grow, develop and become competitive in Canada and in the world.
To contribute to the full development of youth, the Department of the Secretary of State as well is doing its full share in five major fields of activity: funding post-secondary education, the youth participation program, the Canada Student Loans Program, official languages in education and special activities like Voyageurs Canada '92.
The government has a big role to play in education. Although education is under provincial jurisdiction, the federal government's expertise and funding means equal opportunity for all young people in Canada.
[English \
The action plan for Canada's prosperity released in 1992 called for a major effort on behalf of colleges and universities across Canada to become more responsive to the educational needs of Canada.
Canada spends approximately 2.2 per cent of our gross domestic product on post-secondary education. This may at first appear to be a modest amount, however in dollar terms in 1991-92 that amounted to almost $14.9 billion. The majority of that investment comes from the federal government. It reflects our commitment to developing highly qualified human resources which are critical to our future.
March 18, 1993

We support post-secondary education directly and indirectly. Through Established Programs Financing arrangements and other forms of support the federal government will channel about $8 billion into post-secondary education in 1992-93.
Contrary to what my friends opposite may suggest, this government has not cut funding for post-secondary education. We have been forced to impose restraints on spending to control our national debt and we are proud of our government's record in this area. Even in this time of restraint we are well aware of the need for investing in our future. To that end the total funding available for post-secondary education has continued to increase.
Established Programs Financing support for post-secondary education has steadily increased by nearly $100 million in 1990-91, by another $182 million in 1991-92 and by more than $72 million this year. The total Established Programs Financing support for post-secondary education now exceeds $6 billion. This is just basic support for post-secondary education.
The federal government has in 1992-93 forgone some $3.6 billion in tax revenue and contributed about $1.4 billion in cash. The federal government also provides direct support to post-secondary education through other programs. The Department of the Secretary of State is the lead department for co-ordination between departments and agencies for education matters. Without the involvement of the federal government, post-secondary institutions and their students will lose almost $2 billion worth of direct support including $123 million for post-secondary schools directly funded by the government. To put this contribution into perspective there are roughly the equivalent of one million post-secondary students in programs across our country.
Our support for each person registered in a post-secondary education program amounts to $8,000 a year, or about $30,000 for a four-year program. We are investing $8 billion in our future this year. That is certainly not robbing a generation of young Canadians of their legitimate aspirations. That is how we must build a strong and prosperous country.
Supply
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to talk to you about the Canada Student Loans Program. By helping needy students pursue their post-secondary education through the Canada Student Loans Program we are promoting the full development of the nation's youth. Basically, a Canada student loan is an investment in someone's future.

About a quarter of a million students are now in post-secondary studies with the help of the Canada Student Loans Program. More than half of the recipients are women and more than a quarter of the total are over 27 years of age. In every region of our country the Canada Student Loans Program assists needy students with a helping hand. This represents $740 million in Canada student loans for 1991-92, $100 million more than the previous year.
This sustained commitment to investing in the individual has resulted in Canada's enviable rate of participation in post-secondary education, about 62 per cent in the 20 to 24 year old group, second only to the United States at 68 per cent.
The program also contributes to the development of a well educated, skilled and adaptable labour force which is critical to increasing Canadian activity, competitiveness and our quality of life.
We have through the Canada Student Loans Program provided support for students to pursue their educational goals. This is an ongoing commitment to the potential offered by our young people.
This government has also committed itself to modernizing the way we fund and operate the Canada Student Loans Program in order to enhance assistance for needy students and to strengthen the program even further. There is more to post-secondary education than just the hard dollars invested in our future and our young people.

Activities to promote our two official languages are also part of our educational objectives. The Department of the Secretary of State is committed to co-operating fully with the provincial and territorial governments so that minority anglophones and francophones can receive education in their own language in their communities and help other people become familiar with the other official language.

March 18, 1993
Supply
Two major advantages flow from such a commitment. For one thing, it helps fight illiteracy and school dropout by encouraging French and English speaking youth to acquire the skills needed to be competitive. For another, it is clearly advantageous on the world market for Canadians to know both official languages.
About 2.9 million young Canadians have benefited from the Official Languages Program of the Department of the Secretary of State and thus acquired essential skills for our common future. In 1990-91, our provincial and territorial partners invested $3 for every dollar allocated by the federal government to official languages in education. That clearly proves this program's success in motivating not only students but also those directly responsible for the administration of education in the provinces and territories.
According to a study of the Official Languages in Education Program conducted in 1992, the provinces and target groups believed that federal aid was absolutely necessary at all levels of the education system. Furthermore, 74 per cent of the parents questioned in that study want their children to learn both official languages in school. The promotion of official languages is a key to encouraging young Canadians to pursue higher objectives by calling on skills in which the federal government has invested.
Several components of the Official Languages in Education Program have yielded amazing results. For example, about 7,000 students take part in French or English immersion courses every summer, thanks to a special program.
Every year about 1,200 students have part-time employment as teachers' aides in courses in French as a first language, under the Official Languages Monitors Program. In addition, the program helps some full-time monitors in rural or remote regions.
The Official Languages Promotion Program funds some 20 organizations of young francophones throughout the country that are committed to fighting assimilation and promoting the feeling of belonging to Canada.
In Quebec the program helps young anglophones continue to play an active role in their own language in Canada.
In co-operation with all provinces and territories, various programs promote the growth of post-secondary institutions in all parts of the country that teach the official languages. Right here in Ottawa, the Department of the Secretary of State and the ministry of education of Ontario are helping to finance the Cite collegiale. This is not just a small grant; it involves creating a whole new French college in Ottawa.
The Cite collegiale is one of many projects in which the department is taking part all across the country. The government is interested in the issues that concern all Canadians. It is not satisfied with mere rhetoric; it does not hesitate to participate financially and to act on the strength of its many years of experience, competence, planning and deep commitment.

Speaking of actions, the government is also involved in outreach youth through our other programs. Many of our programs target the youth of this country as a principal audience or as a specific subset of the main audience. Programs like Stay In School encourage high school-age young Canadians to graduate from high school. Funding for 10 official language minority community radio stations speak often to the youth in their own language. Also, our involvement directly creates 200 jobs.
The Education Support Branch of the Department of Secretary of State is also responsible for funding Canadian studies learning materials. The department co-operates with the Department of External Affairs to ensure the effectiveness of our participation in international education forums and activities. As well, the Education Support Branch is involved with non-governmental organizations that are active in education. The Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada, the Canadian Association of University Teachers, the Canadian Federation of Students, the Canadian Federation for the Humanities, the Conference Board of Canada and the Canadian Education Association are just a few of the organizations with which the department deals on a regular basis.
March 18, 1993

We must also mention our work with the Commonwealth Youth Program, the International Council for Canadian Studies and Canadian Information Centre for International Credentials as part of our UNESCO commitment.
The Department of the Secretary of State produces hundreds of publications for educators, teachers, administrators and resource centre staff. As an example, they produce the Guide to a Good Exchange which shows voluntary organizations how to maximize the over-all success of a reciprocal student exchange with tips on fund raising, organization and planning.
The department works with people who have disabilities through National Access Awareness Week and the Disabled Persons Participation Program. Both include youth involvement.
The Native Citizens Directorate programs feature community-based programs that target the youth of this country.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we come to our special programs. My friend opposite should be familiar with Voyageurs Canada 92. Indeed, his own riding of Haldi-mand-Norfolk was paired with Dartmouth, Nova Scotia as part of the Voyageurs Canada 92 program. One hundred young Canadians between the ages of 16 and 21 left Dartmouth and travelled to his riding last summer to experience life in another part of Canada first hand.
Another 95 young members of his riding travelled in turn to Dartmouth to see life through Nova Scotia eyes.
On behalf of the Secretary of State, I would like to thank the hon. member for joining us to create such exciting educational experiences for our leaders of tomorrow.
In all, nearly 28,000 Canadians took part in Voyageurs Canada 92 as part of the Canada 125 celebrations. Thousands more people, not just young Canadians, but Canadians of all ages, felt the effects of Voyageurs Canada 92 through the joyous exchange of stories and memories and even the learning that comes from spending time with someone from a different part of the country.
Supply
Since 1986 some 100,000 young people participated in exchanges funded under the OHC. An example is the Encounters with Canada program at the Terry Fox Centre here in Ottawa, which brings approximately 3,000 students between the ages of 15 to 17 to enhance their knowledge of Canada and, again, a greater awareness of our country by participating in one-week workshops.
One participant in the exchange organized by the YMCA, another organization funded under the OHC program, had this to say: "Many more of these programs are needed to help bring Canadians together. We have so much in common yet all we ever hear is what divides us. These exchanges are vital".

The hon. member for Haldimand-Norfolk moved a motion which says that this government has robbed a generation of young Canadians of their legitimate aspirations.
Perhaps he did not know the extent of this government's commitment to advancing our youth. Perhaps he did not know that we have invested $8 billion in post-secondary education. Perhaps he did not know that the government has forgone $3.6 billion in tax revenue from post-secondary institutions, thus helping these institutions make better use of their resources. Perhaps he did not know that a quarter of a million students in our colleges and universities are counting on help from the Canada Student Loans Program to obtain their certificate or diploma in order to build their career, to build our country.
Perhaps he did not know that 2.9 million young Canadians are gladly learning our two official languages. Our country will benefit from that long after my colleague has left his seat in this House.
Perhaps he did not know that 1,200 university students have part-time work as teachers' aides in first language French courses, not only in cities and towns but in rural communities and remote regions.
Perhaps he did not know how committed the Department of the Secretary of State is to helping official language minorities in colleges and universities, not only through financial assistance but by providing expertise in specific projects, together with the provinces and territories.

March 18, 1993
Supply
Perhaps he did not know that we participate in thousands of projects, large and small, with teachers, administrators, researchers and students to find solutions together, through dialogue and information sharing, to common problems in post-secondary education.
Perhaps he did not know that the Secretary of State has relations with very many organizations, volunteer groups, associations, government departments, companies and countries in order to provide the best possible quality of post-secondary education in Canada.
Perhaps he has even forgotten that about a hundred students from Dartmouth visited his riding to get a glimpse of another part of the country.
Hopefully, he now understands this government's deep commitment to education much better. It is not only a commitment to post-secondary institutions, primary schools, rural schools or schools for the French or English minority, but also a deep commitment to the whole process of acquiring skills to succeed in life.
Our Canadian youth have not been robbed of their legitimate aspirations.

We have provided as many tools as we can to train the scientists, teachers, technicians, politicians, lawyers and decision-makers of tomorrow.
We give the youth of Canada the encouragement, the head start and even our trust and silent hope for a better future. We have tried to describe for all who come later a path that will see our country grow and prosper. By investing in the individual, we ensure that every young Canadian has a fair' chance of success along the path.
We are giving our young people the education, the courage, the skill and the common sense to make their own way along their own road to success, whatever that might be and in whatever direction that might be. That is the record of the Department of the Secretary of State.

Mr. Speaker, I want to sincerely thank the hon. member for his speech. It was a non-partisan speech that outlined a
number of the programs the government is bringing forward. Frankly, we do not have any problems with a number of those programs because they do address a number of needs out there now, not only in terms of education, but keeping young people in school.
What we question is the real commitment of this government to actually recognizing the problems with generation x. There is a whole generation out there that has no hope for a job. They have no hope for a proper education and they have no hope that this government even recognizes the seriousness of the problem.
Preventive medicine is always a good direction to go. I do congratulate the government for putting money into keeping kids in school. As we know, that is a very important area. I congratulate the government for the Voyageur program which the hon. member talked about.
All the people from Haldimand-Norfolk had a fabulous time in Nova Scotia. They got to learn some of the problems and the unique differences within this country by going on that program. I hope the hon. member by saying that is suggesting the program is going to come back for another year. I did not quite hear the hon. member say that but I would hope that maybe one of his colleagues could clear that up for us. I know there are people in our area who would be more than willing to again volunteer their time and services to make sure the program continues because it was very worth while.
My question to the hon. member is this. The hon. member knows that the federal government, having all the physical, fiscal and all the trade responsibilities, really has the responsibility to control the economic direction of this country. The federal government has the ability to set a labour force, to set the training, to set the education for a whole country and for a whole group of young people who just do not have that opportunity.
Does the hon. member agree that the whole problem with generation x, and I know the hon. member understands what I mean when I say that, is that whole lost group which is hundreds and hundreds of thousands of young people who are unemployed, many of whom have never had a first-time job, and if you look at the statistics many have never had a first-time job, has increased dramatically over the years?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I wish to thank the hon. member for his introductory remarks. I must say I have a lot of empathy for our Canadian youth. I have three children myself, two of whom are teenagers, and I must say it is a full-time job to bring them up and ensure they can look forward to a promising future.
1 also want to take this opportunity to mention my personal involvement in the Voyageurs Canada 92 Program. We were twinned with not one but two ridings: Nipissing in Ontario and Brandon-Souris in Manitoba. Every time, I personally picked up our visitors at the airport and went to say goodbye to the young people representing my own riding before their departure.
I also took part in many of the activities that were organized in my riding, together with the families that opened their homes to our visitors. We are now completing our review of this experiment and as far as I am concerned I have nothing but praise for this initiative, and I am sure there are people who will want to repeat the experience.
Regarding further programs or incentives to help tomorrow's youth, I reviewed the measures we introduced since 1984, including the Stay in School Program. I was involved in a number of seminars attended by teachers, parents, people from the various LCSCs and students themselves. These programs are constantly being adjusted to make them right for our young people. The department is also constantly seeking new initiatives to ensure that we have young people we can be proud of tomorrow. We must also bear in mind that we inherited a deficit that weighs heavily on this country and puts a number of restrictions on what we want to do. However, we intend to spend and do what we can to ensure that our youth can look forward to a promising future.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to comment on what I have been hearing this morning and put a question to the member for Quebec-Est.
This morning I have heard a lot of doom and gloom from members of the opposition with regard to youth and their future. I think it is somewhat too negative, to be blunt about it. I say that in the context there are great opportunities out there for all Canadians and in particular young Canadians.
We all know that the western world is going through some difficult times but I want to remind the opposition and I want the member for Quebec-Est to reflect on this. In terms of a global society, if you wish, Canada is doing pretty well. In fact this year our economy is expected to outgrow or outperform the economies of every country in the civilized world by something in the order of 3.5 per cent. That figure is very significant because jobs and opportunities for all Canadians, young and old alike, grow or are created from that. It is something I want the member to reflect on.
There is another point I want to make. I want to take the opposition to task on this in terms of our commitment to training and our commitment particularly to the university sector and post-secondary education. I want to pass this statistic along to the member for Quebec-Est to comment on. Every year we transfer to the provinces $6 billion for post-secondary education. Even in times of restraint-we are going through times of restraint now- we have increased that funding and not diminished it. In fact we have increased funding to the post-secondary sector through the provinces by 43 per cent from 1984-85. We are also providing $1.9 billion in training and research to the provinces.
I want the member to reflect on that and comment on what we are doing as a government given our fiscal resources.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad the hon. member mentioned that Canadian policies and programs are often quoted as an example in other countries, and that is quite true.

March 18, 1993
Supply
I purposely did not mention transfer payments to the provinces earlier on, and more specifically the amounts allocated for occupational training because my speaking time was limited, but I am glad the hon. member raised this very important point. With these payments, the provinces and the territories can spend the money directly on training for our young people.
Mr. Speaker, in recent years there was a trend toward one-shot programs for our young people, which were not that successful. During the 1984 election campaign, I often said that the only permanent thing about these programs was the signs. In fact, the signs stayed up well after the programs ceased to exist and all the money had been spent.
Subsequently we made a number of radical changes by redeploying this money in ongoing programs, where program development and investment impact can be evaluated.

Mr. Speaker, I am very proud that the Liberal Party has chosen to spend a full day in the House of Commons to acknowledge the plight of our youth. What better way to spend taxpayers' money than on our youth, their future and Canada's future.

I repeat, the best investment we have is our young people, who represent the future of this country. We must create programs aimed at reducing and eventually eliminating the dropout problem by providing these young people with the training they need to find permanent and satisfying employment.

Last week Statistics Canada reported that since the last election from 1989 to 1992 there were 409,000 fewer young people who had jobs. The UI rate for young men between 15 and 24 years of age is 19.6 per cent in Canada. The UI rate for young women between 15 and 24 is 14 per cent.
What does that mean for our society as we try to come out of this devastating recession? The very people who should be full of energy, full of hope and willing to take risks to reach the positive goals they have dreamed about-the young people of Canada-are disillusioned.
They feel undervalued. They are a generation of lost hope.
That is why I am particularly pleased that the Liberal member for Haldimand-Norfolk has put forward the motion that this House condemn the government for policies-maybe he should have said lack of policies-regarding jobs, job creation, post-secondary education and job training and retraining that are having the effect of robbing a whole generation of young Canadians of their legitimate aspirations.
If this Conservative government had spent more time in the past eight years considering long-range goals for our country, our youth would not be in the terrible situation in which it finds itself today.
It is not just the young people. What about their parents who have sacrificed to allow their children to stay in school? These are parents who want the best for their children. These parents want to see some prospects of a healthy, profitable and productive future for their children.
When the UI rate for our youth is twice that of the rest of society, what does that say about this Conservative government? The Conservative ministers and members have jobs but they do not have vision. For eight years they have not had the vision to see that the youth are our future.
The Prime Minister and the finance minister keep saying that 9,000 new jobs were created last month in Canada but the truth is that we lost 5,000 full-time jobs. The figure 9,000 comes from the creation of 14,000 part-time jobs minus the 5,000 full-time jobs lost.
The government has let the youth of this country down. It is saying that it will give them part-time jobs flipping hamburgers but it is doing nothing to find them full-time jobs.
The hon. member for York North and the Liberal Senator Philippe Gigantes travelled across Canada and then prepared a comprehensive report Agenda For Youth. This task force has made many great suggestions. One of them is that the federal government in concert with provincial governments, the private sector and voluntary associations commit to eradicating illiteracy and innumeracy among Canadian youth. How can we expect our youth to attain the highly skilled jobs needed in the world today if they cannot read or write or if they lack the necessary mathematical skills?
March 18, 1993

Another suggestion is for the federal government to adopt a tax base system to encourage workplace training. Instead of always blocking the way with disincentives, the Liberals suggest using incentives to encourage private enterprise to participate in training our youth.
With the Liberal Party ideas do not stop with the report. The Liberal Party under our leader has already committed to some definite measures for the future of our youth to make these recommendations a reality. In his January 27 speech the Liberal leader stated in part that a Liberal government will work to create a national apprenticeship program to help keep young people in school and to help the transition to work. He also stated that a Liberal government will establish a Canadian youth service designed to allow young Canadians to gain skills and work habits.

Has the government thought of the future? Has it thought of our young people, who are about to begin their adult life without hope, without jobs, without adequate training and without interest? Why not set aside some money for youth development and training?

The youth of Canada know the devastating record of this government. We certainly heard from the Liberal youth task force travelling across Canada. In my riding of Hamilton Mountain students from Mohawk College and from McMaster University spoke of their lack of hope for the future. Students in the high schools in my riding-Barton Secondary, Caledon, Crestwood, Hill-field Strathallan College, Hillpark, Sir Allan MacNab, St. Jean de Brebeuf and St. Thomas More schools-all know the precarious future they face.
That is a good enough reason for young people of this country to defeat this government in the next election and to vote for the Liberals who have a vision for Canada and who want to participate with the youth of Canada in realizing the potential of our great country and every Canadian in it.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest-but

She mentioned long-range planning in her speech. I tell her most sincerely that we have engaged in longterm planning for the youth of this country and for the economy. I take her to task on that. When I say that, I go back to the task force report that she obviously has with her this morning. It was set up by the Liberal Party regarding youth, the economy and employment opportunities, et cetera, to which she has alluded.
I am wondering if that document has been tabled in the House or made public. Perhaps it has and I hope that it has. I suggest they probably will not form the government. The Canadian people will determine whether that happens or not.
In that tax reform package they really do discuss within that document what they are going to replace the GST with. Unfortunately, they will not make that document public. As I have mentioned, I hope this document is made public and I hope it is tabled here in the House so we can examine it.
I will caution the member that much of what the member had to say has been stolen from our pages and our government. Mr. Speaker, it will not take me a minute to answer.

The hon. member is right. The Canadian people will decide. It was the youth of Canada we listened to. The youth of Canada told us they are not satisfied with what the present government is doing.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have the opportunity to participate in this debate. The motion deals with education, job training and retraining.
Over the past four years there have been many discussions on all sides of the House on the whole question of education, training and retraining. Members of the House of Commons had and still have concerns about the state of the economy and about what is happening in the community in terms of the lack of opportunities and so on. I do not think anybody would disagree with that. However, I think where there is disagreement is that actions speak louder than words sometimes.
So far we have not seen any kind of tangible action taking place, whether we talk about the government in terms of dealing with the question of job creation for youth, training, or transfer payments when it comes to education.
In terms of the NDP, what we have seen day after day in the province of Ontario unfortunately is an attack on the youth of Ontario when it comes to post-secondary education when it comes to grants and when it comes to tuition fees.
Rather than spend my time talking about the lack of action from both the federal perspective as well as the provincial NDP perspective, I want to share with this House some of the things my colleagues and I have done in the past.
In terms of our caucus position on this whole question, a youth report was tabled a number of weeks ago. For those who would like to obtain a copy they can call any Liberal member of Parliament.
The report contains many interesting points. We call for the establishment of national apprenticeship programs. We call for the establishment of some sort of an organization that helps out youth in terms of those who want to participate in the work force. We have tax incentives being proposed in order to help business create jobs. Those are the kinds of things that are needed.
What we need more than anything is a cohesive and co-operative approach that would deal with the whole question of education. There is one segment of this whole debate I would like to focus on specifically. That is the question of literacy.
I know my colleagues have spoken very nicely on education and post-secondary education. I want to share with the government some of the proposals I am working on as someone involved in the area of literacy. I want to divide my proposal into four sections and specifically tell the federal government what its role should be in this whole area.
Over 38 per cent of Canadians are considered to be functionally illiterate. As a result of that these people have difficulty finding jobs and the jobs that are available may not be available to them. The cost of illiteracy is in excess of $10 billion, which is almost 25 per cent of the national deficit.
What is lacking now? We lack a national literacy strategy on the part of the federal government. We do have the National Literacy Secretariat. It was set up five years ago and is in its last year now. The minister made a statement sometime around December saying he wanted to continue with it. However, we have not seen one single penny being allocated in terms of funding. We have not seen any kind of additional commitment with respect to the secretariat for the next five years and beyond.
The government has to look at this whole area of literacy with a little more seriousness than it has done in
March 18, 1993

the past. We can no longer just give lip-service to the communities out there. We need to set out a strategy.
This is what the minister could do. He could establish a strategy at the national level. It would include the policy of national minimum standards on literacy and an awareness campaign. These standards on literacy should be set and met at all levels from elementary school and through to employment training. As well, it has to address the question of adult training programs. Only then can we ensure good quality literacy training across Canada.
We cannot just set up an agency and hope that everybody will run to the agency asking for help. We have to have a pro-active secretariat. We have to give the secretariat the needed funds. We have to give it the tools it needs in order to move out further.
We have to set up a strategy whereby we could bring the relevant groups together. We could bring in the provinces, the private sector, the school boards, the special interest groups, the families, the illiterates and organizations working on behalf of illiterates. We could get them together and move forward.
An ad hoc approach is not going to help us. It is not going to get us out of the ghetto we have found ourselves in for the past few years. We need to have action. That is something my colleague from Hamilton spoke about so eloquently. There is a definite lack of action.
We have a literacy secretariat that is in place for five years, but what about the next five years? Why do we not provide the secretariat with a long-term funding formula so it does not have to come begging to the minister every five years? Why do we not have an act of the House of Commons that will make the secretariat a permanent body of this government? Why do we not have an act? As it is now, there is only a government memorandum concerning the setting up of the secretariat. There is no action plan other than a statement in terms of what will be done in the next 10 years and what we are going to do beyond the next 10 years.
I know the government has stated that it wants to increase the level of literacy. It wants to increase the number of people who graduate from school. What are we doing to achieve that? What is the mechanism the government would set in place in order to do that? It spent over $20 million on consultation which is wonder-
Supply
ful. I have to commend it on that because I think it is imperative to have the consultation. What is next? Where are we moving from here?
My colleagues and I are alarmed at the high unemployment rate our youth are faced with. An unemployment rate of 15 per cent to 25 per cent is incredible. It is a national crisis when our youth find themselves on the streets without jobs and without opportunities.
Those are the kinds of issues we are concerned with. Those are the kinds of issues we would like to see the government take action on.
We are also concerned that when the government is in the process of introducing any kind of act the people affected by that act are not asked for their views on it. I refer here to the loans act when it was introduced and put in place a few weeks ago. The student body was not allowed to appear before the committee to give its reaction to the proposals.
It will be recalled that the government made a commitment last year. The minister promised in this House on February 25, 1992 that the government would eliminate the 3 per cent tax on student fees. Have you heard anything on that? It has been one year and there has been no action on this issue.
I know my time is up and we are approaching one o'clock. All I wanted to say is for the country's sake let us sit down and come up with some sort of cohesive plan to deal with the question of unemployment, with the question of youth, with the question of education.
Let us stop this harassment we are embarking on when it comes to our student population. I believe that what we are doing is harassing our youth rather than approaching them with a proper plan.

March 18, 1993

Mr. Speaker, this morning at the transport committee amendments were made to Bill S-8, relating to the Motor Vehicle Safety Act, which will provide Canadian consumers with a consistent Motor Vehicle Safety Act and related safety regulations while providing the Canadian automotive industry with a level playing field when competing with the U.S. industry.
I want to commend the three ministers of transport who addressed these concerns with me over the past three years, the officials from the department who have shown great patience, and the members of the committee from all parties who worked together to give Canadians a high standard of motor vehicle safety.
Under the amendment all vehicles whether imported or non-imported will be required to meet the same safety standard, thereby eliminating the double standard which has existed since the implementation of free trade.
If vehicles do not meet this standard at the time of importation they will be required to be upgraded prior to licensing. This will assure Canadians that they will continue to have the highest standards of safety in the world.

Mr. Speaker, the situation in Bosnia-Hercegovina continues to degenerate. The insidious practice of expulsion and the senseless and brutal genocide of people based on their race and religion must be stopped.
Last July the immigration minister promised relaxed criteria to allow 10,000 refugees in to Canada. Yet so far only slightly more than 1,000 have arrived. Improved terms and conditions are needed. As well, let us consider the example of Israel which is settling refugee families on an interim basis until peace is restored.
As international citizenry we should have learned from past massacres that it is our responsibility and our duty to avert this kind of devastation, but when it occurs we must act expeditiously and with human compassion.
Canada and the international community have been slow to move in the face of this genocide, this abominable, this deliberate ethnic cleansing.
In 1993 how can civilized nations afford to allow this practice to continue and not act? Remember, silence can be deafening and the women are being tortured.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate Merfin Elygienic Products Inc. of Delta for the astounding contribution this firm has made to B.C.'s exports.
This company's German parent established in B.C. in 1986 and now operates a 151,000 square foot plant employing some 65 people. The company introduced a unique European paper-making technology to North America and has plans to spend up to $18 million in the next two years on increasing plant capacity.
In 1992 company sales were up 60 per cent over 1991, and the company has established itself as a major exporter. Nearly 80 per cent of its 1992 revenues were generated by sales in the U.S., Europe and the Pacific Rim.
Congratulations to Merfin Hygienic Products Inc.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to protest the loss of Air Canada jobs in Winnipeg.
Diners Club/enRoute, an operating division of Citibank Canada, thanks to the sale of enRoute last year, announced last week that it will be creating 100 new jobs in the Montreal area.
What it did not announce was that approximately 80 current enRoute jobs in Winnipeg will be lost as a result of this same decision. Winnipeg's history of losing out to Montreal continues unabated and no voice on the government's side is raised on its behalf.
March 18, 1993

I am told that another 48 Air Canada jobs in Winnipeg are at risk because of a scheme by Air Canada to farm out its revenue accounting systems program to an American company, using a system developed by Air Canada employees which they thought they were designing for their own use.
Remember when we used to have a publicly owned national airline? Contracting Winnipeg work out to a U.S. firm would have been unthinkable then. Now the whole city seems to be dispensable.

Mr. Speaker, it is with total disbelief that I read today in the Montreal Gazette that the Minister of National Revenue will not even attempt to collect over half a million dollars in GST payments that were supposedly mistakenly refunded to the yes committee in last October's referendum.
As an excuse he said that the yes committee is officially disbanded so the government simply cannot collect.
Now Canadians finally realize where the GST is going. It is going to line the pockets of the big three: the Conservatives, the Liberals and the New Democratic Party. It is absolutely unconscionable that the taxpayers of Canada, a majority of whom voted against these three parties in the referendum, are actually subsidizing these parties through the loss of this revenue.
The minister should resign for funnelling GST tax dollars to his friends involved in the yes committee's activities. At the very least, the Tories, the Grits and the socialists should pay back the money they owe to the Canadian taxpayers.
My constituents say no once again to the yes committee. They say: "No you may not get off GST-free. Pay your debts".
5. 0. 31 QUEBEC

Mr. Speaker, earlier this week I gave Parliament evidence that Jacques Parizeau expects that a sovereign Quebec will be reliant upon France.
As well, in an article in the June 1992 issue of The Financial Post the member for Lac-Saint-Jean said that as a sovereignist he, and I quote: "expects a lot from France". Perhaps Quebecers should be asking the member for Lac-Saint-Jean what the sovereignists expect from France and what Quebecers will have to give up for this.
The Parti Quebecois and the Bloc Quebecois are insisting that Quebec can make it on its own, yet the evidence suggests otherwise.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday I questioned the Minister of Justice on what preventive measures were being undertaken by his government to address the root causes behind criminal behaviour.
I also drew the minister's attention to a letter sent over four months ago that was signed by myself, MPP Tony Ruprecht, metro Toronto councillor Derwyn Shea and city councillor Chris Korwin-Kuczynski. It pleaded with the minister to apply federal resources to fight the rampant drug and sex trade in Parkdale-High Park. To date we have not received a response to our request.
For the minister's benefit, I invite him to attend a public forum that I am co-hosting along with the hon. member for Scarborough West next April 3 at Metro Hall in Toronto.
In the meantime, I will leave the minister with the comments I received from one of the senior citizens in my riding. I quote: "Seniors cannot go out at night. We deserve to go out and enjoy music and the arts but we are victims in our own homes and feel that we are in jail permanently".

March 18, 1993

Mr. Speaker, the Canada-U.S. free trade agreement has thrown open the doors to opportunity for industry and workers in my riding of London-Middlesex.
I point to the Kaiser aluminum extrusion plant recently built in London, Ontario. Kaiser's Canadian sales manager says the Canada-U.S. free trade agreement made it all possible. The elimination of a duty on aluminum products crossing the border has eliminated a major obstacle.
Sixty per cent to seventy per cent of this plant's production will be sold in the U.S. A further example of the free trade agreement's benefits is the $675 million U.S. deal between General Motors' diesel division in London, Ontario and the leading U.S. railroad company, Burlington Northern. General Motors will build 350 locomotives by 1997.
Free trade is paying off. Just ask my constituents. Mexico can also be good for Canada. Let us get on with the deal.

Mr. Speaker, the New England Journal of Medicine has pointed out that it costs 40 per cent more per patient hospitalized in American hospitals than it does in Canada. It also points out that not only are our costs lower but that we have lower costs in administration, that we use high technology much better, and that we target children much better than the Americans do.
I am delighted with my leader's comments about his commitment to the Canada Health Act and its five principles, as well as his unfailing commitment to medicare in Canada and its universality.
I am really quite disturbed, as are many other Canadians, by the comments of two leadership candidates of the Conservative Party suggesting that perhaps user fees or universality of medicare would be compromised. As well, there was another leadership candidate who agrees. This is very disturbing to Canadians.
I might also add that the Filmon government in Manitoba has decided to cut and slash hospital programs. I think it has not seen this particular study.

Let us leave the scalpel in the hands of those who know how to use it and not in the hands of those who do not know what to do with it.

Mr. Speaker, we have some good news for small, weekly community newspapers and paid circulation magazines. These businesses would have faced a drastic increase in postal rates on March 1, 1993. Rate increases will be limited to 10 per cent a year for the next three years as opposed to a 50 per cent increase.
This agreement between Canada Post and Communications Canada also guarantees that Canadian paid circulation magazines will benefit from a gradual transition to full commercial rates. Additional rate increases will be limited to 3 per cent, 5 per cent and 5 per cent over the next three years.
Also, the replacement program for paid circulation magazines which was to be implemented in 1994 has been postponed until 1996. This government recognizes the important role small weekly newspapers play in advancing community participation, and this is just one more positive program we have put in place to continue to foster pride in small communities.

Mr. Speaker, it has now been established that there is really no difference between provincial Tories and federal Tories.
Shortly after the current election campaign in P.E.I. began the provincial Tories ran ads that were so revolting and insulting to the people of P.E.I. that the Tories had to withdraw the ads.
Now the member for Halton-Peel, who could be the next Conservative Prime Minister of Canada, wants as part of his economic policy to eliminate the province of Prince Edward Island from Confederation.

March 18, 1993

This is the same MP who with two of his pals slithered into Summerside in July 1989 when the Tories closed CFB Summerside. Now he wants to close the province.
Does this potential Tory prime minister reflect current Conservative economic thinking? What province will follow? Newfoundland? Saskatchewan? Manitoba?
Barbara Yaffe, Vancouver Sun suburban editor, quotes future Prime Minister Garth as saying:
One of the ways he would lead us out of the shadows of debt would
be to cut government bureaucracy in ways that would curl hair from
St. John's to Victoria. Does a tiny province like P.E.I. really need its
own government?
I call upon the Prime Minister to apologize to the people of Prince Edward Island on behalf of this government and to repudiate the remarks of the member for Halton-Peel.

those people who hate trade unions, like The Financial Post, how wonderful it has been to see CAW members getting a chance to exercise democracy.

Mr. Speaker, let us examine another exciting day in the life of the PM,-that stands for puppet master of course.
First the PM, the puppet master, from his throne in the mansion, not the one in Westmount but the one on Sussex Drive, pulled the strings to orchestrate his own dynasty.

No matter. From the mansion, the one on Sussex Drive not the one in Westmount, the PM finally convinced Fuzzy to enter the race to give the performance some legitimacy.
