speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of all Canadians, especially those whom I have the honour to represent in this House, I want to express how indignant and angry we feel about the cartoon published this morning in the Montreal Gazette.
This drawing incites violence.
It is a disgrace to Canadian journalism. Its author, Terry Mosher, is trampling underfoot what we Canadians hold sacred: respect for the individual, the family, democracy and plain common sense. Nothing can excuse this cruel and disgusting attack on the Prime Minister and his family.
I call on all my colleagues to protest energetically to the man responsible for this indignity and those who allowed it to be published. Freedom of the press exists here as elsewhere to defend values, to express what is noble and beautiful in the human being.
Those who use it to foster hate, to encourage violence, must be denounced; such people are a poison that threatens democracy. The real butt of the cartoon we saw this morning in the Gazette is the mean, small-minded, sick man who drew it, Terry Mosher. The Gazette and its editors have made a mockery of what a newspaper is supposed to be.
Mr. Speaker, sometimes we get our hands dirty reading a newspaper, but those who read the Gazette this morning felt that their very dignity as human beings was sullied.

Mr. Speaker, free trade was responsible for Bill C-91, one of the worst pieces of legislation to ever pass through this House.
Extending drug patent protection to the fabulously wealthy pharmaceutical companies at the expense of all Canadians, present and future, is a typical Tory fiddle. But is this government content? No. Now it has proposed a ban on 64 herbs and plants because of an obligation in the free trade agreement with the U.S.
Canadians have been using these healing medicinal alternatives for decades. Aboriginal peoples have been using them for centuries. Yet when the multinational pharmaceutical companies are involved Tories know what is best for us all: Level the playing field by clearing any competition even if it is a backyard botanist.
It is time for a change. Let us abrogate the disastrous U.S. trade deal, squash the proposed Mexican deal and chuck this money-grabbing Tory government out on its
ear.

Mr. Speaker, I refer today to the scandalous and odious incitement to violence and assassination being proudly printed in this morning's Montreal Gazette.
This is a disgrace. It is a black eye for Canadian journalism and a crime against the fundamental Canadian values of decency and mutual respect.
Given Mr. Mosher's well-known proclivities, I would have thought he would have been the last person in Canada to deal with the question of violence so lightly.
I call on the owners, the publisher and the editorial staff of the Montreal Gazette to apologize to all Montrealers and to all Canadians for this vile and hostile message carried in today's caricature by Terry Mosher.
Given the enormous tragedies that have befallen Montreal at l'Ecole Polytechnique and Concordia University, only a truly sick mind could find anything humorous in a suggestion that such insane violence be repeated against the Prime Minister of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell the Prime Minister that I share the views expressed by his colleague concerning this morning's cartoon. It was not called for. But we have to ask a question of the Prime Minister anyway.
March 18, 1993

Yesterday a report published in the New England Journal of Medicine said that Canadian medicare is 40 per cent less costly than the American system. Whereas in Canada everyone is covered freely, in the United States 30 million people are not covered. It is reported that the Canadian system is as good and even more effective than the American system.

Mr. Speaker, I have not read the statement to which my hon. friend refers. I will be happy to take a look at it.
The general sentiment my hon. friend has expressed in regard to the Canadian health system, with its imperfections, is that it remains one of the finest in the world. I have had the occasion recently to indicate that to President Clinton and to others. I think that is a view that would be widely held by Canadians.
I suppose if anyone wanted to campaign for any job if there were a vacancy, this might not be the best platform one might want to adopt. However, I am not aware that anybody has considered adopting that.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:

I would like the Prime Minister to comment on this: It is one week before the election in P.E.I. One of the leadership candidates has suggested that we should abolish the province of Prince Edward Island. Is that a new idea that will become part of the Tory program very soon?

Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister who may have forgotten that the present Leader of the Opposition was responsible for putting the Department of Veterans Affairs in Prince Edward Island.
Provincial governments are saying that they have to impose very tough budgets on their populations because of this government's policy of off-loading its own debt and deficit problems onto the provinces.
Will the Prime Minister start a new approach based on working with the provinces to deal with these kinds of concerns? This would be instead of simply dumping or off-loading the government's own problems on the shoulders of the provinces through capping and cutting vital transfer payments for key programs like post-secondary education and health care.

Mr. Speaker, the problem of course is not one of off-loading. The problem is that certain provinces waited too long to cut back on their own rate of increase in expenditures.
When we came to office program expenditures in Ottawa had been increasing at a rate of 15 per cent a year for 14 years. We cut that down to below the rate of inflation to 4.1 per cent over nine years.
Provinces-for example, when the new NDP government came in in Ontario-increased expenditures in the neighbourhood of 13 per cent a year. They finally realized that you cannot spend your way out of this kind of problem so they are now beginning to do what they should have been doing some years ago. I congratulate them for that.
I want to point out to my hon. friend that the suggestion that there has been off-loading is misleading. Major transfers to Ontario will grow at an average annual rate of 6 per cent.
The major transfers to Newfoundland exceed $1.4 billion and have been growing at a rate above the rate of inflation, namely 5.1 per cent for nine years.
Transfers to Saskatchewan have been growing at an average annual rate of 7.4 per cent when the Government of Canada has kept its own expenditures down below 4 per cent. We are transferring to Saskatchewan
infinitely more on a percentage basis than we are expending here in Ottawa. I congratulate the premier of Saskatchewan. Lie has finally come to the view that the policies we have been seeking to implement here are the right ones both for Canada and Saskatchewan.

Mr. Speaker, what the Prime Minister is talking about is really an ad hoc approach to crises created by previous budgets of his government.
Will the Prime Minister convene a high level federal-provincial conference to develop a new approach to federal-provincial fiscal and financial relations? This approach would be one that gets away from making the provincial taxpayer bear the burden of what in fact amounts to mismanagement and resulting off-loading, no matter how the Prime Minister describes the situation.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to get into an argument with my hon. friend. The figures are there and they are either right or wrong. He can examine them and stand up in the House and say that the information I have just given to the House is wrong.
The fact of the matter is that our present difficulties were generated by program expenditures at the federal government level which increased at this-
It is our fault.

My hon. friend says: "It is our fault". For once he is right. It was abusive spending which now has to be brought under control at all levels, the federal level, the provincial level and the municipal level. That is all we are saying.
There is enough blame to go around for everybody. I do not think anybody gets any advantage in saying: "It is not my fault, it is yours", or vice versa.
Clearly, the country has to come to the view that we have been living beyond our means for too long and it must stop. I commend those provinces and those premiers who have come to the realization that program expenditures cannot increase at a rate of 14 per cent a year when productivity is increasing at 1.8 per cent and revenues are increasing at 4 per cent. It does not work. It leads to the kind of deficit and crippling of our growth that we have seen. Only these kinds of economic and fiscal policies can ensure we get out of that on behalf of our children.

Mr. Speaker, when we were in Washington, D.C., we learned that the proposed labour side deal has three options. The first option protects no one. Hear, hear.

Heureux qui comme Ulysse a fait un beau voyage!

My hon. friend knows full well that Canada's labour standards are among the highest in the world. These have always been enforced and will continue to be enforced by the Government of Canada and have continued to be through the free trade agreement and will be through NAFTA. My hon. friend should not worry about matters that have been resolved and will continue to be defended very vigorously and I think well.

Mr. Speaker, possibly the only thing more dangerous is a Prime Minister who has taken a trip to the United States and is telling us that these side deals have very little, if anything, to do with Canada.
We know there is no enforcement of labour standards in Mexico. We also know the track record of the government when it comes to protecting Canadian workers. It is bad, bad, bad. I would ask the Prime Minister again to protect Canadian workers. Is he going to do that or is he going to abandon them in his rush to sign and ratify the NAFTA agreement?
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, what we are submitting to the House for consideration is a treaty among Canada, Mexico and the United States. It is a trade treaty designed to increase commerce between the three countries. The entire international experience being that as you lower barriers and tariffs you tend to create more wealth.
I truly do not understand the preoccupation of the socialists with Mexico in the following sense. Socialists demand that we give more and more foreign aid to developing countries. Mexico is saying that they are a developing country but they would rather not have handouts. What they would like is an occasion to trade into a developed market. NAFTA gives us that opportunity to trade, thereby raising the collective wealth and living standards of Mexicans so that they can better fulfil their responsibilities toward their own citizens.
What we are trying to do is allow Mexicans to share in the wealth of our continent as we create new jobs for Canadian citizens.
I would have thought that the socialists would get behind the idea that we can become more prosperous in Canada while helping our neighbours share in that prosperity.

What is scary is a Conservative demonstrating altruism. What did the Mexican bishop say about the North American free trade agreement? I think what we have seen here is a demonstration of paternalism.
The Prime Minister says he has some doubts about the wisdom of the side deals. The Minister for International Trade says we are willing to consult. The Minister of the Environment says that yes, of course, it is incorporated in the deal.
We want to know who is speaking for Canada and why Canadians should have any confidence in the negotiating stance of the government?

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to offend ecclesiastically anyone but my hon. friend can assume that Mexican bishops are not speaking for Canada. The people speaking for Canada are the authorized ambassadors who are there negotiating skilfully on behalf of the people and the Parliament of Canada.

We have some remarkable public servants, very talented and able, who are there today representing the interests of the government and the Parliament of Canada. Mr. Speaker, the government must know that the removal of interprovincial trade barriers is a major requirement if Canada is going to benefit from freer trade whether hemispherically or globally.

Madam Speaker, I

welcome this opportunity to draw the attention of the House to the events that will take place on World Francophonie Day on March 20 and to the importance of this anniversary for Canada and the international community.
Canada is privileged to be a member of our two major international families, the Francophonie and the Commonwealth.
In both families, one traditionally headed by France and the other by Great Britain, Canada's status is such that it is able to create support for the fundamental values it is intent on sharing with all its fellow members.
Canadians should realize the importance of Canada's membership and its unique status within the Francophonie.
Canada has every reason to be proud of belonging to this great francophone family whose membership today includes 47 countries and governments, spread over five continents and representing more than 400 million people.
This forum, initially dedicated to cultural and linguistic issues, has since 1986, thanks to the summits of heads of state and heads of government, expanded to include political, economic and development co-operation. Much of the credit goes to our Prime Minister who was involved since the very beginning.
This year there will be many events to mark this anniversary. Activities will mostly emphasize youth, starting with a conference of youth ministers next June in Senegal, to provide for a lasting follow-up to the New York summit which the Prime Minister of Canada had the honour to co-chair with the President of Mali.
In July, the second Francophonie games will take place in Marseilles and Aix-en-Provence, where more than 400 young Canadians will represent Canada's sports and cultural elite. Finally, the fifth summit of heads of state and heads of government from countries where the French language is commonly used will be held in October in Mauritius.
Madam Speaker, like the events organized by Quebec and New Brunswick, those that will take place today in Ottawa are intended to make more and more Canadians aware of the Francophonie and its influence throughout the world.

March 18, 1993

What we are here to discuss today is what the federal government is doing to help people acquire the skills that they need to bring their talents and abilities to the work force. That is the issue.
We live in a changing world in which new technologies are being developed and new economies are emerging. This means that the nature of work is in transition and increasingly we must compete on a global basis.
If we are to compete individual Canadians and Canadian businesses must be in a position to take advantage of the opportunities that lie ahead. Our policies will ensure that. Our policies will ensure that our work force will have the necessary skills to operate our factories and businesses.
Make-work programs, which are called for every day by the New Democratic Party and at times by our friends from the Liberal opposition, do not address these issues. The solutions of the 1970s, make-work projects, lulled Canadians into believing that we can buy the illusion of prosperity. That is the Liberal way. They have tried it. They still rise in this House and call on us to borrow more and mortgage the future of all Canadians even more, and even those who are not born yet.
They say mortgage their future more, borrow more, pass more, create again the impression that we can buy prosperity and that we can buy the standard of living Canadians enjoy.
The Liberal way and the socialist way do not work. Proof of that-
Has your method worked?
Let me talk; your turn will come. Madam Speaker-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would ask the hon. minister to address his comments to the Chair. If both sides avoid making comments directly to one another we will avoid unseemly language which should not be heard in the House of Commons.

Certainly, Madam Speaker. In fact, I am anxious to check the "blues" to see if I said anything unseemly. If I did, I withdraw it.
I want to make the point that make-work programs do not address these issues. They were the favoured measures of the 1970s and they did help remedy downturns in cyclical industries. I am ready to acknowledge this. However the problems we face today are more complex and require different and innovative solutions.
Now we do not wish to offer Canadians band-aid solutions that do not solve the problem. Instead we have instituted working at creative solutions and I tell my colleagues in the House that indeed they are making a difference.

We are providing more training to Canadian workers. We are helping Canadian industry meet its human resources needs. We are doing more with less, abandoning passive income support programs for more productive measures. As the saying goes: "When I look in the mirror I get upset, but compared to others I am doing just fine".
If you compare Canada to other industrialized countries, OECD members for instance, you can see that 75 per cent of income support funds are active rather that passive. In Canada, with the Unemployment Insurance amendment bill we passed a few years ago, we have now managed to activate 15 per cent of those funds to help people meet the challenge of acquiring new and greater skills. We are redirecting that inactive money-because we are paying people to do nothing-by providing them with help and enabling them to get the training required to re-enter the labour force, which discriminates much more today than it used to in terms of necessary skills. We must find new approaches.

Rather than offer Canadians more handouts, we want to give them the ability to find and keep stable employment. Our financial commitment in that regard has grown significantly to keep pace with this important priority.
March 18, 1993

In the 1993-94 fiscal year some $3.8 billion has been allocated for employment programs and services. That is considerably higher than the $2.1 billion spent in 1989-90. Now when talking about $3.8 billion it has to be looked at from the perspective of the government policy of reducing expenditure.
If we look at the cuts that my colleague the Minister of Finance announced in December, people will realize that not one penny was cut from the training funds, the money that can really help Canadians reintegrate into the labour market. That is a clear message that this government affords the highest priority to human resource development.
My colleagues were talking earlier about the education moneys that are being transferred over to provinces. The funding of $3.55 billion in 1992-93 enabled close to
700,000	Canadians to participate in Employment and Immigration Canada's labour market programming. In 1993 $2.21 billion will be directed toward training and adjustment measures for UI claimants. As I said earlier, the training this funding will provide is essential to help the unemployed find new jobs.
We introduced Bill C-113 which is before this House as we speak. It is hoped that later this week it will be considered at report stage. Bill C-113 will introduce measures which will no longer allow those who voluntarily quit their jobs without just cause and those individuals fired for misconduct to claim UI benefits.
I understand that these changes are opposed by the Liberals and the New Democrats. They say that Canadian taxpayers should pay unemployment insurance benefits to people who voluntarily without just cause choose to become unemployed. That is the position of the Liberal Party.
Hard-working Canadians are being asked by the Liberals and the socialists to please continue paying benefits to people who choose to become unemployed. Not those who have to quit a job for just cause, and many do. Those people will be fully protected. But no, for those who have no reason whatsoever, no provocation, no just cause, they say: "Please Canadian taxpayers, pay these people benefits".
These are policy positions of the opposition that result from-

-how could I say it so as not to offend you, Madam Speaker-their connection with or their commitment to
Supply
such special interest groups concerned with the higher interests of the nation. I think this is a sad and alarming position to take, but ultimately the Canadian people will decide between the solutions they have put forward, those reactionary solutions, and the ones put forward by a progressive government and a progressive party such as ours.
These measures allow us to do more in terms of training as they make money available. Instead of paying benefits to people who, by the way, are free to quit their jobs without just cause-I am not stopping them. The point I am making is that we should not be asking money from our neighbours to pay for these benefits because we need that money to provide yet more training to those who truly need it, that is the workers who did not choose to become unemployed but were laid off all over the country because of the economic restructuring and technological changes we are facing. Some would like us to ignore these changes.

They wish away problems. But you cannot wish away problems or reality; these things are happening. We have to have the tools in place which help our people to be able to meet those challenges. Those policies are expressly tailored to do just that.

Government is aware of the specific problems facing especially long-standing employees, those men and women who suddenly find themselves with no job after having been employed by a company or having worked for their employers for a long time.
In the near future, we will be implementing a special program for people who get laid off after having had stable employment. In many cases these people lost their jobs because of the world-wide industrial restructuring that is taking place. More often than not plants close suddenly. There is no way of warning the workers well in advance. So they do not have time to prepare, to retrain or to look for another job.
In this new program we at Employment and Immigration Canada will be spending $300 million to provide assistance to these men and women to help them re-enter the labour force as quickly as possible. This assistance will include teaching job-search techniques, administering skill tests and providing information on the labour market, and it will enable some of these people to get the training required to get a job.

March 18, 1993
Supply
Under the new program Employment and Immigration Canada will establish partnerships with certain communities and businesses to set up local adjustment assistance committee. Through these committees we will be able to promptly provide laid-off workers with the services they need. As you know, Madam Speaker, some groups are specifically targeted for assistance under Employment and Immigration programs, but we have never paid particular attention to permanently laid-off workers who have had ongoing employment for long periods of time. That is what this program is intended to do.

The previous member talked about the school dropout situation. I want to say that our stay in school program has been an outstanding success. If colleagues remember, the current Minister of the Environment was the minister responsible for youth when he introduced this stay in school program for all of Canada. It has been an outstanding success.
An increasing number of young people in this country are choosing to stay in school and upgrade their education. Between 1989 and 1992 the proportion of youths 20 to 24 years old who were full-time students rose from 48.4 per cent to 53.5 per cent. This is a tangible sign that young people are recognizing the importance of a good education.
My colleague has already informed the House about this program and our other programs for youth employment, but we are doing more. Canada's young people have access to all employment and immigration programs. Our figures show that in the 1991-92 fiscal year a little over 196,000 young Canadians took advantage of our other programs. Regular program spending for the youth segment of our clientele amounted to almost $740 million.
Now this is serious money. This is taxpayers' money. It is devoted to that segment of the population which probably has the heaviest burden on its shoulders, that of assuring the future social, cultural and economic success of this country.
Education is not just for the young. The government places a great deal of importance and urgency on building a private sector learning culture in Canada.
We all know that in the past in order to be successful in the regions of Canada all that was needed were strong arms, a strong back and strong legs and a hard-working spirit. In that way we were able to create this country and create wealth. We have been able to develop a standard of living almost unequalled in the world. Canadians have a high standard of living and we did that mostly with our muscles and partly with our brains.
Nowadays that is over. Future wealth will only be created by that grey matter called a brain. That is the reality. That is why human resource development, training and education must be at the forefront of the government's concern in this country. This government has shown its true colours in terms of education and training by the amount of taxpayers' dollars it is directing to this crucial issue.
I said that education is not just for the young and it was important that we create this learning culture in Canada as a result of the reality we face. We have a dedication to the renewal of this great nation's human resource infrastructure, that is, our people and their skills. The quality of the work force in Canada will be and is a direct determinant of our future prosperity.
The Canadian people know that manpower retraining is essential if our country is to compete on the international market but they are concerned that we may be out-done by our major competitors. In Canada the private sector has to invest more and realize that only through manpower training can their competitiveness, their productivity and their success on the global market be ensured.
Madam Speaker, you are signalling that my time is almost up.

I would love to have been able to speak about the central initiative which I predict will revolutionize the way in which the private sector considers training and education in this country. This is a $352 million initiative that is already in place and will be expended in a major way in the next few months for the benefit of Canada.
March 18, 1993

For all these reasons this House should never condemn the policies of this government because they are exactly what Canadians need.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will tell you that I have a lot to say about the minister's last sentence.
I want to ask him two questions. In his speech the minister referred to the POWA program and said that he cares a lot about those who after a number of years lose their jobs because the company for which they were working shuts down. Therefore, his government according to him wants to implement programs to help these people and ensure that such a thing does not occur. I will get back to this issue.
As for POWA, is the minister aware that right now workers are laid off and will not be able to get the benefits or the help provided for older workers because of a rule in this program? For two or three years we have been presenting petitions to have this rule changed. For example, on the island of Montreal if a company closes down and has fewer than one hundred employees these people do no qualify. It is not their fault. They are not responsible for the plight of the company. They are old enough to qualify for this program. The number of years during which they worked in the industry makes them eligible but because the company must have a minimum of 100 employees they are penalized. In cities such as Montreal, Toronto and all the metropolitan centers which have been experiencing very hard times in the last few years because of the recession workers who are 55 years old are unemployed, cannot get jobs and find themselves in a difficult situation precisely because of this POWA program set up by this government.
Madam Speaker, I have a second question for the minister. He says that the policies put forward by his government and by him as Minister of Employment are bringing good results. I would like to tell him about some of those results, especially in Quebec. In our province, 29 per cent of the population is under 30 years old. They account for 50 per cent of part-time workers and 72 per cent of workers earning the minimum wage. Thirty-three per cent of Quebecers on welfare and 42 per cent of Quebecers on unemployment insurance are less than 30 years old. The drop-out rate in Quebec is 36 per cent, the highest in the country. Is that the result of the minister's policies?
Supply

Madam Speaker, I did not realize that I would have the opportunity to give my learned colleague a course on constitutional law this afternoon. If the member wants to criticize the Quebec government in this House for the drop-out rate, so be it.
We all know that education is under provincial jurisdiction. Unless the member wants to be so partisan as to blame this government for the school drop-out rate in Quebec or elsewhere in the country, we should recognize the concerted efforts made by the government of Quebec and the Government of Canada to fight this drop-out problem.
I fully agree with my colleague that a drop-out rate of 36 per cent is unacceptable. However, it must be recognized, and I am sure he will agree, that more and more Quebecers and Canadians from all the other provinces are aware of how important it is for young people to stay in school. In our government's prosperity initiative I had the privilege to meet groups of parents and educators throughout the country who are trying to address the issue of drop-outs. There is a consensus in this country on the need to restructure our education systems and adapt them to the needs of our young people; this is in addition to other social measures which must be taken to help our young stay in school.
The hon. member referred to the Program for Older Worker Adjustment which is the responsibility of my colleague the Minister of Labour. Personally I can say to the Liberal member from Montreal that the best way to impoverish a nation is to idle its human resources. It is true that people who, unfortunately, are laid off, sometimes after many years at their job, have real difficulties retraining or finding a new job. It is with this in mind that we have introduced this Program for Older Worker Adjustment. We want to help those workers.
It is true that there are eligibility rules and that not everybody can retire. Personally, I think that we should try to benefit from this older workforce. In this country we treat our older people as if they had nothing more to offer society. We want to put them away somewhere and tell them to stay there. I say that our collective challenge as a society is to find out how we can benefit from the experience of those people. These older workers are an immense pool of talent, experience and wisdom, and we should see how we can make them re-enter the workforce so that the whole country can benefit from their experience.

March 18, 1993
Supply
I do not think that the solution is to find how we can make everybody retire at the age of 55. These people are loaded with talent; they can do a lot for their country. The programs which we need should rather seek to bring them back into the workforce and thus help the younger people who need their experience.

Madam Speaker, I would like to agree with the minister in one of the comments that he made a little earlier that one cannot wish away problems. Ele is absolutely right but one does not deal with problems that exist today by creating more problems.
He mentioned Bill C-113 and that voluntary quitters should not be entitled to benefits. The magnitude of that statement goes far beyond just the cutting off of their benefits. It also deprives them of the opportunity to get training.
The penalty the minister is imposing on these workers in this bill is overkill. The punishment must fit the crime. One cannot send someone to jail for stealing a chocolate bar, for goodness' sake, and the status quo certainly serves the needs of the Unemployment Insurance Commission in terms of people not having the ability to quit their jobs.
The minister talks very eloquently about education and about our older workers. He says that we should establish ways of utilizing that education. He is absolutely right, we should. But putting them in the ranks of the unemployed through the loss of their jobs is not the way to do it.
We have an educated work force. The problem is that there are no jobs to go to. I think that this minister rather than attack the unemployed should be looking at ways of attacking unemployment and creating jobs whereby we could use the talent of those older workers who are now out of work as a result of his government's economic policies.
We have university students who are graduating every year with no jobs to go to. Yet we are saying that we have
to train people for jobs. The whole point that the minister is missing is that there are no jobs for these people to go to.
I would like to ask the minister this: Why does he not look at ways of encouraging industry to hire people?
The mining sector is hurting. There are ways of creating employment in the mining sector. We have miners who are out of work. There are thousands and thousands of years of work experience going to waste. Why not do something for the mining industry in order to put these workers back to work so that they can train people to keep the mining industry thriving and prosperous?
Why not look at those kinds of solutions to the problems instead of creating more problems by introducing bills like Bill C-113?

Madam Speaker, very briefly, I have two quick points. First, when the hon. member refers to the need for industry to create jobs, he asks what one does to create jobs. We entered into a free trade agreement. We entered into a North American free trade agreement because this is about trade.
We cannot sell our goods to this great population of Canada of 27 million people. We have to trade with the world. By trading and by opening the trading doors of Canada to the world we are creating jobs.
On the other point he made, we talk about the level of unemployment. In this country, in 1991, an interpretation of our help wanted index reveals that 300,000 jobs went unfulfilled in Canada because people did not have the skills.
My point is this and I will close on this: The modification to the Unemployment Insurance Act that takes people out who quit their jobs voluntarily without just cause leaves more money to train those unemployed Canadians who will get the skills to create and fill those
300,000	jobs that went unfulfilled.
I am sure that if the New Democrat member thinks this thing over he will want to applaud the measures of Bill C-113.
March 18, 1993

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise in the House to discuss government policies regarding jobs, jobs creation, post-secondary education and job training and retraining, because of the severe implications that government policies are having on Canada's youth.
Those of us who have recently been to our ridings will know from recent experience the pain and suffering being caused to so many youths across this country. As the motion indicates whole generations of young Canadians are being robbed of their legitimate aspirations to have a job, to build a life and to work in Canada.
The only amendment that I would think would be appropriate to a motion like this is that this House should condemn the government for continuing Liberal policies regarding jobs, jobs creation, post-secondary education and training and retraining because that is really what has taken place.
Over the last 18 years we have seen cutbacks from the federal government to the provincial governments under both Liberal and Conservative federal governments that have had these extremely negative implications on the provinces. It would be appropriate just to indicate what those cutbacks have been because they have had a major impact on the provinces. I will indicate the impact that they have had on my province of Saskatchewan.
In 1975 the then finance minister, the member for Vancouver Quadra, placed a ceiling on federal contributions to help with post-secondary education. In 1977 the then Liberal government backed away from equal costsharing for health and post-secondary education with the provinces with the introduction of block funding. The federal share of spending has continued to decline.
In 1982 the Liberal government then removed the revenue guarantee program for health and post-secondary education transfers to the provinces. As a result of that, $6 billion has been cut from post-secondary education. In 1983 the six and five guidelines placed restraints on post-secondary funding. That has also taken millions of dollars out of moneys available for the province to fund such a critical aspect of any program which will provide opportunities for youth, that of post-secondary education.
Supply
In the last eight years of Liberal federal governments there were four initiatives which cut funding to the provinces for post-secondary education.
The Conservative government continued these cuts. In 1986 Bill C-96 changed the formula which escalated federal spending on health and post-secondary education. Instead of spending increasing at the rate of GNP, i.e. at the rate at which our wealth could permit it, the legislation reduced the rate of increase to gross national product growth minus 2 per cent.
This to the end of the 1980s had been costing the provinces $2 billion annually. In 1989 the finance minister proposed a further change to that formula and funding was reduced to GNP minus 3 per cent. In 1990 the budget imposed a two-year freeze on per capita transfers to the provinces for both health care and post-secondary education. In 1991 this 1990 freeze on health care and post-secondary education funding was extended for another three years and we are here debating that issue today.
We have clear joint responsibility on the part of Liberal and Conservative governments to attack the opportunities for Canadian youth to obtain post-secondary education. We could also talk about the cuts to other programs, to the cap on CAP and so on. These programs also have taken money away that the provinces needed to carry on the very important programs which will enable our youth to have a future and play a part in Canada's future.
In case anybody has any doubt about the magnitude of these cuts to established programs financing for health care and post-secondary education, in 1992-1993 because of this dozen or so measures by Liberal and Conservative governments, $247.9 million was taken out of the province of Saskatchewan.
Agricultural program cuts, primarily in the last three or four years, took $215 million out of Saskatchewan, and other programs such as unemployment insurance offloading, manpower agreements, young offenders, legal aid, RCMP, criminal injuries compensation and so on-the list is quite long-added another $75.2 million which was taken out of the province of Saskatchewan in 1992-1993 alone. The total is some $538 million, which is around the deficit of the province of Saskatchewan for that year.

March 18, 1993
Supply
Had the federal governments, Liberal and Conservative, not made offloading a priority, not transferred the debt load from the federal government to the provinces, the province of Saskatchewan last year would have had a balanced budget.
This year in spite of those offloading dollars the province of Saskatchewan will have reduced its deficit by almost half. The cost of these offloading measures, of the province having to take over more and more of education, is that other programs have to be cut.
This can only be described as short-sighted. The government's rhetoric is of course quite right. We do have to become a better trained, better educated work force. We do have to create jobs so that that training can be put into effect. We do have to compete in a global market and it is not getting any easier to do so. That is all the more reason why we should commit ourselves again to funding policies which assist job creation and job opportunities for our youth as well as for other Canadians.
The reason we should recommit ourselves to adequate funding for post-secondary education is that it is not appropriate and not good for Canada. It is not good for Canadians that our post-secondary education system is becoming ever more elitist, ever more difficult for those of lower incomes to have the opportunity for post-secondary education. The whole support mechanism is making it more and more difficult for ordinary Canadians to go to universities, colleges and technical institutions.
Summer job programs have been cut back so it is more difficult for a student to obtain a summer job. Student loan opportunities are cut back so there is not enough money available to borrow in order to go to university. It is almost a vicious circle: Student fees go up because of federal government offloading; one after another it becomes more and more difficult for Canadians to obtain post-secondary education.
We need initiatives to encourage job training and retraining, to ensure that businesses in Canada carry out their fair share of training, which they have notoriously not done in the past by comparison to other countries, and in particular by comparison to those countries with successful economies. All these things need to be rethought and developed so that Canada's youth have the opportunity both to obtain the skills they need in order to participate in the work force and have job opportunities available to them so that they can use those skills to best advantage.
Over the last 15 years or so we have seen a gradual erosion, as I have pointed out, by both federal Liberal and Conservative governments in moneys and support available for those skill training programs and for education programs. We have also seen a move away from a commitment to job creation. We have seen an obsession with deficit control, both under the Liberal government-that is what the six and five guideline was about-and an obsession with inflation rather than an obsession with job creation.
Indeed, what that obsession with inflation has meant is that people have been deliberately put out of work in order to reduce inflation. That is not the way to get Canada's economy moving again. We all know that little will be achieved in terms of development unless we take seriously the need to educate our youth, to provide opportunities for their education and to provide job opportunities for them afterward.
I would like to take one step back because we all know that one of the problems we face, and the minister made mention of it just recently, is that we have an extremely high dropout rate within our school system. In fact we do not have a particularly enviable participation rate of college age students in our universities in comparison to, for example, the United States, which is embarking on a major campaign to increase the participation rate, while we are increasing student fees and making it more difficult for students to go to university.
One of the reasons why Canadian school children drop out of school at the rates they do is because of poverty. We all know we have one million Canadian children living in poverty. We have 1.6 million Canadians unemployed and 2.6 million Canadians living on social assistance. Not only is this a huge social problem but a waste of economic resources. Until we address the major problem that our economy, our society, is not geared to providing opportunities for all Canadians but is geared to ensuring that 4.2 million Canadians have no opportunities at all, we will never change that system. We need to take a different route.
The minister talks about the benefits flowing from the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and NAFTA. What we should be doing rather than giving up control of our economy to our large multinational corporations who do not give one whit about Canada or one whit about creating jobs, is taking control of our economy ourselves for the benefit of Canadians. It is not only for the benefit of Canada but for the benefit of those Canadian youth who need jobs and opportunities for the future.
March 18, 1993

We know from all the records that large multinational corporations operating in Canada have reduced their work forces over the last 10 to 12 years and continue to reduce their work forces. We know that large corporations in Canada generally have reduced their work forces. Those large multinational corporations, of which the government is so fond and has been prepared to ease their sphere of activity through the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and now through NAFTA, are the ones that are driving down employment and cutting back on jobs.
That is why we need to take control of our economy. There are ways of doing it. There are ways of taking charge of our economy. We do not have to give up control on the way as we have done. We all know that free trade began, not with the Conservative government, but with the Macdonald commission of the Liberal government. The whole plan for free trade was set out by Mr. Macdonald and his colleagues. It was then eagerly adopted by the Conservative government. It is not accidental that these things have worked in that way.
Only the New Democratic Party has been consistent in demanding that Canada's economy be controlled by Canada for Canadians. There are things we can do. I will not go into them in detail now but one of them clearly involves us taking charge of our education system, turning it into a system and making it work.
We must ensure that we invest more money in research and development rather than less. We should ensure that government works with business and labour in an effective way to plan the direction that Canada can take rather than just let these things be decided willy-nilly by the business community. It had led us into a situation of 11 per cent and 12 per cent unemployment, a million children living in poverty, 2.6 million people on social assistance and 1.6 million unemployed. That is where these policies have taken us.
What we need to do is take back control of Canada's economy by doing more in the training field, doing more for post-secondary education and doing more in re-
Supply
search and development. This money will not be wasted.
It is money invested in the future. No sensible government, no sensible corporation would not invest in its primary resource, its people. Yet we have seen continual cutbacks by this government and by the Liberal governments before it to those very things which constitute the investment in our future and in our youth.

Madam Speaker, I know the hon. member for Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing has always displayed a concern for those individuals who have to depend on the social system in order to have any kind of standard of living.
I wonder if the hon. member is aware that an organization named the Coalition of Provincial Organizations of the Handicapped made a pre-budget presentation to the Minister of Finance on March 11, I believe it was. Its members expressed some concern not only about being trapped within the social welfare system and unable to get out of it because of the lack of employment opportunities, but they tried to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance two things that were of great concern to them.
First of all the shifting of revenues under the Consolidated Revenue Fund of employment and immigration which they have relied on to a great extent for employment opportunities has been cut back in recent years. Also, the policy of employment and immigration now of increasingly applying training opportunities to those individuals only who are recipients of unemployment insurance benefits has effectively presented a barrier to someone who is not on unemployment insurance benefits from entering into those programs.
They were also very concerned about the transfer payments to the provinces which had to a large extent created a position where they cannot even get assistance under the Canada Assistance Plan because of the cutbacks from the federal level of government to provincial levels of government.

March 18, 1993
Supply
I want to ask the hon. member whether or not he has any information about the amounts of money that are involved in those transfer cutbacks. COPOH, the organization I just referred to, did not have those figures at hand the time they made the presentation. I think they would find that very useful information to have.

Madam Speaker, I thank the member for his question.
While I do not have specific numbers of dollars, the minister is in the House and he might very well have some specifics which he could help us with. However, I want to support what the member is saying and recognize, as I think all members of the House should and most do, that the plight of the disabled in Canada in terms of access to job training and access to jobs is indeed of the most severe nature.
One of the problems that the member just highlighted is an absolutely critical one; that so many of the training programs are available only to those who receive unemployment insurance. Of course the vast majority of those persons who have been disabled and who have not been able to work in the recent past are not eligible for that training. Therefore it becomes ever more difficult for them to take their place in the work force.
The minister might want to comment on that. It seems odd that we would not want to break down barriers to job training rather than put barriers up and why there would not be more effective co-ordination with the provinces to ensure that this training is available.
It might also be that we should hear from the government on why it is taking so long to incorporate into the Canadian Human Rights Act the duty to accommodate that which would make jobs so much more accessible to the disabled and enable them to have the opportunity to work as of course they all want to do.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the hon. member. How can the hon. member stand up in this House and purport to speak with some knowledge about the crucial question facing Canadians in training and not answer to his colleague that over and above the $2.2 billion that is being spent by the workers and employers of Canada to train the unemployed there is also $1.6 billion that is specifically targeted to disabled Canadians, to women, to natives and to minority groups across Canada-$1.6 billion that is being spent.
My other question to the hon. member is the following: Why is the New Democratic Party opposed to activating the passive income security money of UI for active measures to train Canadians? A sure way to help an unemployed person in this country is to help that person acquire more new skills to integrate a labour market that changes by the day.

Madam Speaker, on the first question the minister raised, the issue is not so much how much money is being spent at the present time but how much money is needed in order to address the problem.
Clearly, with the huge unemployment rate among disabled Canadians, the money the minister is speaking of is clearly inadequate to address those concerns. If we are really serious as a country about making sure that disabled Canadians participate in the work force then we owe it to them to put some resources into that. Of course those resources are not just dollars spent, they are dollars that are invested in people which will return to the government in terms of taxation revenue and so on.
Therefore, the question is not how much we are spending. The question is how much money should we be spending and how can we find those resources to invest in Canadians.
The second question was with regard to the use of unemployment insurance funds for training. The minister and I do not disagree on the need for training. The minister and I do not disagree on the need to provide opportunities for those who are unemployed to be trained and to enter the work force. We seem to disagree on the need to have an active, creative and aggressive policy to create jobs in this country, because certainly his government has not done that.
Let us ask whose responsibility it is that those unemployed are unemployed. Is it their responsibility? Is it their responsibility they do not have any jobs, that they do not work? They all want to work. Most of them did work. They cannot find jobs now because of the economic climate, because of government economic policies and, of course, because we live in a difficult world economic environment.
March 18, 1993

If it is not those employees' responsibilities that they are unemployed, why should it be their responsibility to pay to be trained? Why should the training not be paid for those people who are responsible for their unemployment, for it is the government whose economic policies have turned those people out of work?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on a point of order. After Question Period, when I asked the House for unanimous consent to allow the Minister for External Relations to make a statement, I should have mentioned that normally such a statement should have been made at the opening of the sitting, during Routine Proceedings. Because the minister was not present at the time we were unable to proceed.
