Madam Speaker, I am looking forward to entering the debate this afternoon. I am glad to be following the member for Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing because during his comments in the House this afternoon he raised some issues which I believe he will find I will respond to quite well in my prepared remarks. I am going to veer from my prepared remarks and talk about some of the successes I have had the opportunity to participate in over the last few years as a member of Parliament in working with the various programs within my riding of Selkirk-Red River.

March 18, 1993
Supply
I have had the opportunity to work with the very successful stay-in-school program. I would like to compliment a young gentlemen by the name of Trevor Kennerd, a sports figure within the city of Winnipeg area who worked well with the stay-in-school program. He has been a very prominent and significant spokesperson on behalf of it. I would like to talk about the START program later on but right now I would like to commend the people from the North Selkirk school division, the one that I have worked with on a regular basis, because of their participation in the START program. I have been to a number of graduation exercises in the last while. They have always been rather stirring because of the fact that the young people who have participated in these START programs have such an attitude change and seem to be focused on what we would consider the right direction.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration a while back released a paper called Learning Well and Living Well. The Triple-S Community Futures Organization in the Selkirk-St. Clements-St. Andrews area has been participating on a regular basis through a group they call Focus 2000 working toward showing not only the government but the local division and other school divisions the necessity of changing the educational system. There is a nice young lady by the name of Mary Yardveson who is new to our community who has picked up the ball in this specific issue and has run with it quite well.
At the end of the day when this group comes together, it will have a chance to prove that the work of the Community Futures in the Triple-S area not only provides some very significant direction to the local school area but makes significant recommendations and provides direction to education throughout Canada.
I am very pleased and proud to respond to the motion by assuring the House that this government does indeed have the legitimate aspirations of young Canadians fully in mind. One need only look to the National Stay In School initiative for clear evidence of this government's
commitment to supporting today's generation of young people in fulfilling their aspirations.
This five-year initiative was announced in the 1989-90 fiscal year by the hon. member for St. Paul's with a $296.4 million budget and was designed around three main components: a program component, a mobilizing component and a public awareness component.
My hon. colleague, the Minister of the Environment, was instrumental in capitalizing the initiative and in recognizing the critical role all Canadians would have to play in ensuring full economic and social participation for our young people.
I am pleased to note that the author of this supply motion appreciates the importance that training and learning have in job creation and ensuring that the jobs stay in this country.
As we all realize, the job market out there is a highly competitive one. That is why this government has repeatedly conveyed the message to members of the opposition that the solutions lie in fostering a life-long learning culture. The pathway to solution does not lie in continuing to live in the world of 10 and 15 years ago where you could just mortgage the future of emerging generations by increasing the national debt and ignoring the commitment that we as a country must make to learning.
It was our government which realized the importance and the crucial need for having a highly trained and educated work force in place if we as a country are to compete effectively in global markets and have our youth take their place in that work force.
Put that in context. Our government placed a stay-inschool initiative as the cornerstone of our approach to social and economic policy. It was and remains abundantly clear that you must build a solid foundation of work skills as part of the infrastructure for a sound human resource policy. But with three out of ten young people not even completing high school, you can rest assured that youth has a very high priority on this government's agenda if we are to ensure that they will be able to assume their role in society and fulfil their dreams,
March 18, 1993

ambitions and aspirations. Such dreams will be nightmares if the current dropout rate is not reversed.
Throughout the stay-in-school initiative's public awareness component we have been very successful in communicating the state of this issue and its consequences to Canadians at large and to young people in particular. It simply does not serve the future of our young people to enter today's labour market without the benefit of a secondary education and by extension without the employable skills employers are calling for.
There can be no disagreement then that three out of ten young people dropping out of high school is an unacceptable ratio, not simply because of the mid to long-term consequences but because of the personal foreclosure that dropping out spells for each and every young person.
The stay-in-school initiative issued a clarion call when it was launched four years ago. I am proud to say that it is one that has been heard clearly and responded to fully by communities, parents, educators, the general public and young people themselves. This has been done through an array of mobilizing activities carried out under this initiative.
Youth, youth-serving agencies, business, industry, education and labour are working together in a concerted effort and with great innovation to resolve the problems faced by youth at risk of dropping out of school.
No one, least of all this government, is underestimating the magnitude of the problem nor the degree of effort that it will take by all of us working together to ensure successful transition for our youth to the work force of tomorrow.
On the issue of high school drop-outs, I would venture that even the hon. members of the opposition would condone and acknowledge the extent to which this government has enacted an effective catalytic role in bringing the community partners together to redress and resolve this issue.
Members can share the pride that we all have in not only reaching out to youth with our message but also in obtaining the support of business, industry and the general public.
It is worth noting that communities throughout Canada have embarked on programs to encourage school retention. The call to action has been heeded by youth-
Supply
serving agencies like the YMCA, the Boys and Girls Club, Big Brothers and Big Sisters, and business person's groups like the Rotarians that know how to put service to others before themselves, and there are groups like the Lions and the Lionettes, and my favourite, the Kinsmen and Kinettes.
They all recognize the need to positively support the work that is being undertaken in their communities, rather than just standing up and criticizing what is being done. They know how to assume their civic responsibilities. They have put positive action high on their priority list.
Canada's youth deserve the best and that is why our government has supported the action plan of communities through the stay in school initiative's program component. The START program, as it is called, lies at the heart of this initiative.
Through START programs more than 100,000 young people will have received direct services that encourage them to complete their schooling and build their sell-esteem and confidence, which must develop so they can serve the community as best they can.
The kind of services forthcoming for young people under START programs are in the form of innovative interventions. Such interventions have not been developed in a state of limbo. Rather they have been dynamically developed by our community partners in a way that transcends any partisan road-blocks.
We count among those partners provincial and municipal governments throughout the land and corporate partners from all sectors. Practically each day news reports are carried in community newspapers reflecting the concerted efforts being undertaken to support our young people in completing their secondary education.
For example, in Education Manitoba, from February 1993, I read that a new resource kit for teachers and guidance counsellors has been developed under the stay-in-school initiative. It provides lesson plans designed to explore meaningful reasons for students to stay in school.
The first three lessons explore students' career goals and ways to achieve them. A fourth lesson prepares students for a visit from community speakers sharing their experience in the world of work. A fifth lesson focuses on helping students to actively explore their career choices. This is but one example of the resource material developed as a result of the stay-in-school initiative.

March 18, 1993
Supply
If I might once again digress from my prepared presentation, I remember quite vividly a picture in the local community newspaper very recently of the mayor of my home community of Selkirk, Mr. Bud Oliver. He had slipped away from his job as a businessman and was out in one of the elementary schools taking time out of his busy day to talk to young people about what it was like to be mayor and the importance of education.
The Focus 2000 group has built quite an initiative around getting local business people and people of different employment to go to community schools, whether they be elementary schools, junior high or senior high schools, to teach them about their experiences in the work place. I commend those people for those special activities.
This initiative clearly places the needs of this generation and their aspirations as a major priority of this government. The initiative's message that dropping out is no way out has projected far and wide.
Barely a day passes without a newspaper or a magazine, besides highlighting the importance of completing high school, conveying news and commentary about the increasing demands being made by the technology that is changing the work place for all workers and the implications it has for our ability to compete.
The challenge that it presents to our youth is unlike that facing any other previous generation. When we live in the here and now it is difficult to project what skills and abilities the entry level worker will require 10 or 15 years down the road. That is why Canadian youth are showing good judgment and not looking for the quick fix, but rather are placing a high priority on completing their high school education and continuing their studies at the post-secondary level, whether it be through the apprenticeship program, co-operative education pursuits or by attending college or university.
On the subject of quick fixes, I must point out that this government inherited a tremendous debt that nearly crippled Canadians, not only now but in the long term. Yes, we all have to make our sacrifices. We cannot continue to look at short-term band-aid solutions. That narrow vision does not really change the way we do things.
There is nothing I would like more than to be able to guarantee a good job today to every young Canadian. To do so we have to be prepared to stand in the fuller perspective of human resource development as a way of ensuring that Canadians work not only on a short-term basis or on make-work projects, but for the long term. We all have to deal with the needs of tomorrow.
It is for that reason that the stay-in-school initiative encourages youth, parents, communities, business, industry and labour to support locally driven activities. These are being created to mobilize our communities to support and encourage youth in making a successful school-to-work transition. All of us want our young people to be able to assume adult roles beginning with their legitimate aspirations.
It is of interest that with responsibility for the stay-inschool initiative residing with my hon. colleague, the Minister of State for Youth, that his ministerial portfolio with fitness and amateur sport offers a model of coaching which, in the context of the stay-in-school initiative, can and does make a singular difference in encouraging young people to complete their high school education.
It is no accident that the stay-in-school speakers' bureaus which exist in each region draw on the role models offered by young Olympic athletes and aspiring Olympians to convey the importance of training and the relevance of schooling to the world of work. The players of the St. John's Maple Leaf hockey team or Regina from the Western Hockey League are among our stay-in-school ambassadors. Coaching and mentoring form part of the 1,300 interventions presently supported by the stay-in-school initiative.
Just as we cannot expect an athlete to excel without the benefit of training, we cannot expect our young people to enter the realm of work without the skills or attitudes required by employers.
Allow me to reiterate. It is not a quick fix that will make it possible for young people to live their dreams. It takes diligence, dedicated action and action plans. I can assure the House that the action plans undertaken by our partners are starting to point to success under the stay-in-school initiative.
March 18, 1993

For example, in British Columbia alone when the stay-in-school initiative was launched 10 school districts experiencing the highest drop-out rates were targeted. Data gathered to date indicates that there have been significant improvements in student retention rates, with some school districts reporting there may be as much as a 50 per cent reduction in drop-out rates among the at-risk students.
In closing, let me again assure the House most vigorously that the stay-in-school initiative provides tangible, working evidence of the commitment that this government has made to help this generation of young Canadians fulfil their aspirations.

Madam Speaker, I welcome the views of the previous speaker. I believe it would be wrong for any member of this House to disagree with the aims of the stay-in-school initiative.
I am by profession an educator. For four years between 1984 and 1988 when I was not in the House of Commons 1 returned to my profession. I found great changes in the attitudes of students, teachers and parents.
I had been in the House for some 10 years and it seemed to me that the emphasis when I returned was more on how to get along in society, which is a good idea of course, than it was on the accumulation of knowledge.
My hon. friend mentioned that we who are teachers and who have been teachers should have as our goal preparing our young people for the future. With all respect to the hon. member, that indeed should be the goal of education. We should be preparing them for change and for adaptability.
I can cite many studies indicating that the youth of today will have at least five different careers before their working life is over, by that I mean ordinary retirement.
If that is the case, and if our schools are to prepare them for their future, must we prepare them for any one thing or must we prepare them for a variety of things? I pose that as a rhetorical question in this sense: It is my view and it is my contention that the best we can do is prepare them for change because in this technological age, and that was the precise term that my colleague used, of technological change there will be positions in
Supply
existence not 40 years from now but 10 years from now that we cannot even dream about.
How do we measure the success of a student? Is it by the marks we give them at the end of the day? Is it by the fact that when they go out to get jobs this one will earn $40,000 a year and this one will only earn $20,000? I pose the question to the hon. member who has just spoken.
In years gone by we did have standardized tests in Ontario. Let me explain. At the end of grade 13 there were exams that were written right across the province. In order to graduate from grade 13 everyone had to write these exams. From the results we said that this school is better than this school because it turned out more people who had higher grades. I ask the hon. member: Is it his view that we should have standardized tests in all of our schools across Canada?
I refer specifically to the end of grade 8 which is the end of elementary school and then again at the end of grade 12, if that is how many years we have in a particular province. I would like to hear his views on that.

Madam Speaker, I think the questions that have been posed are quite legitimate ones. I do agree that there is a significant technological change going on in the world at this time. In fact I would say there is a technological revolution taking place today that probably is the equivalent or greater than the Industrial Revolution at the end of the 19th century and we have to be prepared to adapt.
I was questioned about how I felt education should take place. There was a lot of commentary about whether getting back to the basics was the right way to go but I think it is a simple term that probably is understandable if one has the basic skills and can then change and adapt.
I agree that there has been a significant change within the school system in the last few years. I think it is not only up to the government and the school system but the parents in general to take responsibility for that. I sometimes think that the parents ask the school division and the school teachers to do more things than they should. I think that a lot of things that take place within the school system should actually take place at home.

March 18, 1993
Supply
We have to give students these skills and we have to give them the ability to go out and perform. If we do not give them these basic skills how are they going to compete or how are they going to further their education?
There is a significant problem within one of my own school divisions. We have a very competent and internationally recognized elementary school called Birds Hill School that has a very progressive program in science and math education.
The problem is that they are looked upon as the black sheep of the family. They are left on their own, which is very discouraging to me and very discouraging to an awful lot of people. When one criticizes the education system then I will say very publicly by way of this commentary in the House that I have never seen anybody circle the wagons more quickly than the education system when somebody comes forward to criticize.
There was talk about standard testing or national testing. I am a proponent of that. I am a proponent of that because it is useful. Sooner or later somebody is going to have five different jobs in their lifetime. Sooner or later those five different jobs might be in five different regions of Canada. If I have to take my daughter who is now in high school from Manitoba and move to Alberta because of a career change, then I want to know that she has the same basics going into that education system in Alberta as she had in Manitoba. One should know that there is a similarity and that the goals to be achieved are very similar.
I sometimes question the attitude of educators who say that because different regions have different requirements that the educational system has to adjust to that. Maybe there is a certain amount of truth to that, but the basic skills of reading, writing and arithmetic are ones that can be carried around.
I have personally written the Prime Minister that I think the education system should be putting a lot more emphasis on delivering those basic skills to all Canadian students. I have no idea how the government puts this upon either the provincial government or the municipal governments, but those are the basic building blocks that you need to move forward in education.
I'll go back to the national standards. I believe that how one uses these national standards is open. My
recommendation to the government has always been that if we create these national standards, whether it is industry or various education systems or universities, they may draw upon them. They may not be forced to draw upon them but there is the knowledge that if Dalhousie University wants to accept students from Selkirk, Manitoba, they know that they have achieved a certain level of education by way of a national test. I appreciate the questions.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, let me first congratulate my colleague, the member for Haldimand-Norfolk, for this Official Opposition motion and I quote:
That this House condemn the government for policies regarding jobs and job creation, post-secondary education and job training and retraining that are having the effect of robbing a whole generation of young Canadians of their legitimate aspirations.
Last February, the unemployment rate reached 10.8 per cent in Canada. In Quebec, it was 13 per cent; in Montreal, 13.7 per cent. Youth unemployment was at
16.7	per cent. That is higher than the Canadian average and higher than the average for the province of Quebec and for Montreal. Earlier, I mentioned some figures for the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
You come from Quebec just as I do, Madam Speaker, and you will understand that I am trying to give an indication of the situation in our province. People 30 years old or less represent 29 per cent of the total population, 50 per cent of part-time workers and 72 per cent of workers earning minimum wage. They also represent 33 per cent of all welfare recipients in Quebec and 42 per cent of unemployment insurance recipients. In the province of Quebec, the school dropout rate is 36 per cent, the highest in Canada.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration was saying that education is in provincial jurisdiction and I agree with him on that point. However, Madam Speaker, we must ask ourselves why there is such a high dropout rate in our education system. Is it because it is not working properly or because our social and economic system is not? Does the minister responsible for employment ask himself that question? If the dropout rate is so high, it is probably because people have lost all hope.
March 18, 1993

When young students see that their brothers and sisters, their friends and neighbours who have studied and gone to university or college are unable to find jobs after graduation, they get discouraged and wonder if it is still worthwhile to stay in school. It is easy to see that the problem lies not only in the education system and that we cannot put the blame on the provinces; it is due to the unbearable socioeconomic situation we have created in Canada. We are losing a complete generation.
I hope the Tory government, which is now embarking on a leadership campaign, will hold a debate on that subject and propose policies which will restore confidence and hope to young Canadians, that will give them an incentive to stay in school and bear with our education system. That way our young people will receive proper training and will be ready to face the challenges of the 21st century.
On this side of the House the Official Opposition and its leader Jean Chretien commissioned a joint committee of Liberal members of the House and Liberal senators which travelled throughout the country. As the member for Saint-Leonard I had the pleasure of welcoming the committee to my riding and the young people of Saint-Leonard took part in the hearings. They had the opportunity to air their grievances, describe their experiences and explain why the present education system is not working.
After touring the country and listening to many groups and individuals, mostly youngsters, that committee made several recommendations and I would like to mention a few.
For instance, there is the creation of a national apprenticeship program by federal and provincial governments, in collaboration with labour and the private sector. This is very important, Madam Speaker.
Earlier the opposition and the government discussed the possibility that workers might have to change occupations at least five times in their career, as studies show. It is therefore important that we have national standards. We know that today the federal minister for trade and
Supply
commerce and his provincial counterparts are meeting in a effort to bring trade barriers down. The time has come.
Much has been said in this House about free trade between Canada and the United States and free trade between Canada, the United States and Mexico but we still do not have free trade within our own country, Canada. It is therefore high time and I think that we will soon see some results. It is important that we do not encroach on provincial jurisdiction. We do not want to take anything away from the provinces but it is important to have national standards for our young people to develop in their own country and to have hope.
Another recommendation concerns the creation of partnerships between the federal, provincial and territorial authorities, the private sector and labour in order to promote co-op programs which allow young people to acquire job experience while studying. We are faced with a new crisis these days. Young people graduate and start looking for a job but invariably they are asked if they have any experience. How can they if they are not given the opportunity to work and gain valuable experience? It would be good to introduce such co-op programs at the provincial and federal levels, between management and the unions and between the work place and the school so that graduating students have not only an academic background but also job experience that would allow them to fully participate in society.
Personally, before I started in politics I had the opportunity to visit Europe and to look at their school system.
In Switzerland, a small company would not have hired a student if he had not studied in a particular technical college with which it had entered into an agreement allowing the student to return to the firm to practise what he learned in school. That is what a co-op system is all about. Not only did that student get a diploma at the end of his schooling but he was also given a certificate of apprenticeship by this particular institution showing that he was ready for the job market, instead of living the tragedy we are witnessing today. Young people sacrifice so much to get their college or university degrees but once they have graduated they are told that they need

March 18, 1993
Supply
experience in order to get a job and it is a serious problem for them.
Another recommendation, Madam Speaker, is the use of tax incentives to promote on-the-job training. It is very important that we do our utmost to encourage businesses to provide training and give a chance to our young people so that they can get a job and benefit from such training in order to remain competitive. This is the 1990s and soon it will be the 21st century; we have to be competitive. We can see big international markets developing, blocks being formed in Europe, Asia and here on the North American continent. If we want to be successful and competitive we must have a highly specialized and well trained labour force. Given the fact that 70 per cent to 75 per cent of Canadian companies are smallsized businesses, which create at least 80 per cent of our jobs, and that those businesses for the most part hire five employees or less, we cannot expect them to have in-house training programs. We have to develop such programs.
So, we hope the federal, provincial and territorial governments, the private sector and volunteer organizations will join us in promoting literacy. It is important. Another tragedy in today's society is all those people who still have trouble reading and writing.
We have to convince our young people that they belong in our society, that they will have a well-deserved place in our society once their training or studies are over. But once they realize that we have to make sure there is a place for them, or they will quit school out of frustration.
I want to touch upon an issue not directly related to youth but which the Minister of Employment and Immigration raised. It is about POWA, a program for older workers. Think about how 55-year-old people, even those who are working, must feel today. With our economy in a state of crisis and our young people having trouble finding jobs, can you imagine how a 55-year-old worker who has just lost his or her job might feel? When a business closes its long-time employees are in a precarious situation. Their job prospects are practically non-existent.
The Minister of Employment has said that the government can no longer afford to pay people to stay home; we need working people in Canada.
I agree with the minister. However, where are the jobs for these people? Where are the training programs to help them retrain and find jobs? If we cannot give them jobs or afford to retrain them, we should at least have the decency to give them enough to live on and raise their families. Many people at 55 still have children in school or at university. They still have a mortgage to pay. In my riding a lot of constituents-I have tabled petitions with 5,000 names on them and I could have a bundle more-a lot of people are asking the government to amend these regulations. There has to be a provision allowing a business with less than 100 employees to take part in POWA.
After several years I still have not figured out the spirit of these regulations. The only reason I can think of is that they want to reduce the benefits the federal and provincial governments give to older workers. But then, if 70 per cent to 75 per cent of Canadian companies are small businesses with less than 100 employees, how can you have regulations that apply only to businesses with 100 employees or more? What happens? In most cases, in urban areas such as Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Vancouver and Calgary, any city with over 500,000 people, this special provision applies and when a business with 100 employes or more closes workers can receive POWA benefits.
It is all right for the government to say it does not want to pay people to stay at home, that it wants productive citizens. I agree, but do we have jobs for these people? Do we have training programs for them? The answer is no to both questions. Once their UI benefits run out, not to mention that the number of weeks of benefits has been reduced, the unemployed are destitute. In most cases-and that is the tragedy-those people do not even quality for social assistance benefits because all their life they saved money, they worked long hours to manage to buy a house and put their children through school. Now they are penalized because after they lose their job, once their benefit entitlement period is over, they have to sell their house and lose everything they acquired from 20 to 30 years of work and sacrifice because they are not entitled to any benefit, not even UI
March 18, 1993

benifits. That is the tragedy we are in with this government's policies.
I hope the Minister of Employment and Immigration and his officials are listening and will amend POWA so that older workers can continue to raise their children and keep them in school, by giving some allowance to those victims of this government's economic policies.

Massive unemployment, low-paying jobs, drugs, youth gangs, violence and a high drop-out rate are the problems faced by youth today. Youth are facing an unfortunate and vicious circle. They cannot find a job without experience and they cannot get experience if they do not have a job. That is the tragedy.
For the record I want to quote an article from The Globe and Mail of January 14, 1993: "The under-25 casualty: Young Canadians are graduating from university and entering the job market only to encounter dead ends and detours. Rough road ahead for unemployed youth".
That is the situation we have today. When we talk about education it is easy to say that because it is a provincial jurisdiction we have nothing to say. In the meantime, we see what is happening.
If the drop-out rate is very high it is because our educational system is not working. It is because young people see their brothers, sisters, cousins and neighbours finishing school, they work very hard to get through college or university, however once they are out there looking for a job they cannot find anything. They are so discouraged by that so they say: "Why should we do the same thing? Why should we continue to stay in school when after so many years of sacrifice they do not want us out there, there is nothing for us?"
That is the tragedy. We have to address that because we are losing a generation. We will lose a total generation. It is very nice to debate about free trade with the United States, and free trade with the United States, Canada and Mexico, but what are we offering those young people? What is the future for them?
The government says: "Oh yes, with free trade we are going to have jobs". So far we have only lost jobs and more and more people are discouraged.
Supply
I remember during the constitution debate a young girl came to my office. She said: "Mr. Gagliano, you are a wonderful member. You talk about Canada, my Canada and I love Canada. But how do you want me to continue to believe in this Canada when I cannot find a job?"
If we want our young people to be proud of this country like we are, we ought to give them hope. They have to have hope for the future. The only way to have hope for the future is to make sure that when they finish school there is a job for them.
Make sure that in getting an education they also receive the necessary training and experience. Then once they finish not only will they get a diploma for their academic studies, but they will also be ready to face the working market, to face the competition. Make sure they are the best trained. Once our young generation is well trained, then and only then can we face the world. Then and only then can we have free trade with any other country. If we have the best generation, the best educated young people in the world, we can face anybody and be competitive.
However, if we continue with the same policies that have been followed for the past nine years there is no hope for our young people. No matter if a free trade agreement is signed, our young people will not find jobs. We will have to reverse this course, otherwise it will be tragic.

May I say, Mr. Speaker, how nice it is to have you presiding in the Chair this afternoon.
It is a pleasure for me to speak on this motion of my esteemed colleague from Haldimand-Norfolk. This resolution is one that is very close to my heart because in my riding of Halifax there are five universities and a number of other post-secondary institutions. Of course because Halifax is a large city, at least a large city by Atlantic standards, there is a large population of young people.

This resolution states:
That this House condemn the government for policies regarding jobs and job creation, post-secondary education and job training and retraining that are having the effect of robbing a whole generation of young Canadians of their legitimate aspirations.
Those are very harsh words. Normally we try to avoid apportioning blame in the general debates in this Elouse. However, every one of us in this House has a very special responsibility to young people, to the youth of this country. Almost anything that comes to mind to talk about that special responsibility could be regarded as a cliche. Except when things are essentially true they transcend the realm of cliche and bear repeating because of their essential veracity.
One of those truisms is that the youth of our country are our future. They are our hope and they are also our salvation. The mistakes of each generation are not necessarily visited upon the next. The things one generation has done wrong can frequently be corrected by the next generation.
However, if we do not provide the atmosphere for that next generation to thrive, for that next generation to plan and for that next generation to dream, then we are not going to improve. We are not going to have a better society. We are not going to see the kind of progress that we have all dreamed of for this country, for our children and for future generations.
Canada's youth are caught in a set of all-pervasive problems. I refer now to the report of the Liberal Party's joint Senate and Commons committee on youth. Our youth are disadvantaged today in two ways: They are buffeted by high unemployment flowing from the current economic recession and they are severely hampered by the continued failure of the federal government to create a better social and economic climate for them.
The committee found that youth unemployment is linked to several factors. The first is technical innovation. The second is that low-paying jobs, which are normally entry level positions, are being phased out in many sectors, meaning that market demands can be met by fewer workers but at the same time nothing is put in place to take the place of those entry level jobs. Third are the pressures of international competition.
What these three factors say is that we are heading into an increasingly globalized economy utterly unprepared. We are unprepared as a country and we are particularly unprepared as a work force. We are most dangerously unprepared vis-a-vis our youth work force.
What do we do? Effectively, and it is an expression my mother used to use and it is called "cutting off your nose to spite your face".
Mine too.

East or west, mothers have the same wisdom.
Young people today want nothing more when they finish their education than to get out into the work force and contribute. All of us here, think of it, just think back and remember what it was like when you knew you had your first job, whether it was a summer job when you were in school or whether it was your first job when you finished your education. Remember what that excitement was like. Remember the anticipation. Remember how you felt, that finally you were entering into that very special world of the adult even if you were, as I was, 16 years old and going to work as an errand girl at the local hospital where I think I was paid $32.50 a week.
There was the dignity of employment and the joy of knowing that you were earning money and making a contribution. You were paying taxes; 16 years old and I was going to get to file an income tax return. I very quickly got over the joy of that particular part of the equation.
I can see by the smiles on all sides of the House that we all remember that. I know equally that we all, every one of us on all sides of the House, want to see that joy reflected on the faces of young people from coast to coast to coast. That is the tragedy.
Here we are in this magnificent, incredible country, with all the things it has to offer, and we are looking at a youth unemployment rate unprecedented in the annals of this country. It is just not good enough. It is not good enough from each and every one of us. It means that each and every one of us has failed. We have failed because we are not handing on to our young people the kind of society, the kind of marketplace, and the kind of opportunity that they deserve. We are not handing on to

them the Canadian legacy that was handed on to us. It is not fair and it is not right.
Shortcomings in government action to deal with these problems have translated into more than 1.1 million Canadians under the age of 18 living in poverty. Imagine that that can be said of Canada in 1993. What a tragedy. What a horror. What a disgrace.
Poverty is not simply an economic problem nor does it simply affect the poor. Employment provides people with a sense of belonging in a community. The fact that people are employed and can make the contribution I referred to earlier has a ripple effect, a spin-off effect in communities across this country that is almost beyond computing. When you are employed, when you are enjoying the fruits of your labours, then you want to make a further contribution to your community. That has been the tradition in Canada.
The employed person, the person who feels that at the very least he or she is making that kind of contribution and supporting himself or herself also wants to make a contribution to the community in other ways, thus making the over-all community a better place for us all.
Statistics Canada reports that between 1986 and the year 2000 the proportion of the work force requiring high skill levels, which means more than 12 years of education and training, will increase from 45 per cent to 64 per cent. But the proportion of young Canadians acquiring such high skills is declining. Our high school dropout rate is a national disgrace. One in three young people drop out of school before gaining the training and skills increasingly required in a knowledge-based society. Here we are, coming into what is known as the age of communication and the age of information, and one in three of our young people drop out of school before they gain the skills necessary.
Children from single parent families and families of low occupational status are streaming into the basic rather than the advanced high school programs. That is the antithesis of the Canadian tradition.
I look at my own family. I look back at my grandfather who, I believe, went to grade 6. I cannot remember exactly but it certainly was not more than junior high school. He eventually became the president of the Mining Institute of America and one of the foremost mining engineers in Canada. His children all went to

university, and God knows his grandchild ended up in the House of Commons.
That is a tradition in Nova Scotia. The children of fishermen, the children of coal miners and steel workers, the children of CN workers and dock workers, went to university because in the Celtic tradition, the Scottish tradition, whatever, education was the most desired goal. The idea that because your father worked in a manual labour job would somehow preclude you from going on to university was nonsensical. It was just not something that was believed in. That is the Canadian tradition.
As I say, I know it from the Atlantic provinces' aspect, but it is the same in Alberta and Ontario and Quebec. It is the same for all of us, we know that. You look at the statistics here in Canada today and the children of dock workers and coal miners and manual labourers are not going into advanced level because they are not being streamed that way.
I do not think that those children are any less gifted. In the long run they are probably more gifted because of the exposure they have had to other educational areas in our society. But they are not going into the streams that will lead them to higher education and higher skills training. This must be changed. We have to focus our goals and targets as a country on education.
Another thing, and supposing the brickbats come from everywhere, we have to get over our constitutional preoccupation with education being a provincial matter. We have to look at education in the broader sense and see that only by co-operation among federal, provincial and municipal governments are we going to solve this kind of problem.
In a speech entitled "Governing in the 1990s" my leader, the member for Beausejour, stated that he would start a national apprenticeship training program to keep young people in school, and help their transition into the work force. That, Mr. Speaker, is one of the areas in which we need to see action as soon as possible.
The transition from school to the work force is probably the hardest transition that young people are going to have to make. There is a young man working in my office here in Ottawa. He is a volunteer, he is a university student, he comes from Halifax, and he goes under the wonderful Irish name of John-Paul Coady. He spent his March break last week back home in my riding looking for a summer job, working every day to ensure that he would have employment this summer to help him go back to school in the fall.

Our young people deserve better than that from their federal government. It is deplorable behaviour in these economic times. governments with all Canadians to develop a concerted plan for young people in Canada.

Madam Speaker, I have been looking forward to speaking on this motion introduced by the hon. member for Haldimand-Norfolk.
What we have been talking about today in the field of education is not only what goes on in a classroom. We are really talking about partnerships in a knowledged society if you will. It encompasses more than just a classroom. It spreads out its arms to encompass our industry, our technology, our science. In a word, it touches on every aspect of our society.
Education in my view is the key to social justice and economic progress. Only a society which values knowledge, innovation and skills can expect to compete in international trade with those nations that have placed highest priority on educating their young people.
Research and development leading to new products and advanced materials, telecommunications and environmental technologies will radically transform the foundations upon which national economies exist today. It is now commonplace that almost all factors of production can be mobilized anywhere in the world; Third World countries, north, south, east or west. Today and in the future the most important of these factors will be the quality of human resources. Education and skills are imperative for success in both a competitive domestic economy and in a global environment.
The challenge to Canadians will be to translate understanding of this fundamental principle into concerted and sustained action. There is much to be done.
Close to one-third of Canadian students do not finish secondary school. That is appalling. A shocking number of young Canadians are illiterate and this is unacceptable. Too few young people are competent in science and technology. Only one-third of students finish post-secondary education. Many of the remaining two-thirds of young people do not receive the skills training necessary
March 18, 1993

to compete in a rapidly changing economy, indeed, in a rapidly changing world.
Even though many youth do not plan on post-secondary schooling, the Canadian system of vocational and apprenticeship training is haphazard at best and in my view has achieved very poor results. University funding has been slipping at a time when many other nations have redoubled their efforts to provide high quality education for their young people. Why have we not been doing the same thing?
Action is urgently needed. That students traverse the educational system and emerge illiterate shocks Canadians. It shocks me and it should shock those here in this House today. In fact, for over a decade the Science Council and the Economic Council have warned that students were failing to reach minimum levels of literacy in reading, writing and the sciences.
How can this be? How can this be acceptable in this age of 1993? What is the price of illiteracy? The price of illiteracy is potential unemployment. In future labour markets it may be impossible for illiterate or marginally literate youth to make the transition to high skills levels demanded by technological advances in the most competitive firms.
There have been many warnings over the potential fate of any industrialized nation which does not adequately address the problem of illiteracy. As they say, the chickens are going to come home to roost unless we do something about it now.
It is troubling to me that the federal government has responded to public concern over illiteracy by decreasing support for those programs designed to address this problem. The argument that Canada may already be spending too much on education does not bear close scrutiny.
Based on a percentage of gross domestic product, the GDP alone, Canada spends the most on education of all the OECD countries. However, Canada's expenditures on education as a proportion of the GDP per capita are only somewhat higher than average among OECD members. Clearly, Canada needs to achieve better results with the money it does spend, as the hon. member from the other side has just said.

I believe that provincial governments and public services are perfectly capable of evolving and applying solutions to a national problem within their jurisdictions. So does this committee believe that interjurisdictional co-operation will happen and that it will help.
