The House resumed from Friday, February 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Allmand that Bill C-285, an act to amend the Citizenship Act (oath of allegiance) be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Human Resources envelope.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise in debate on this private member's bill, Bill C-285. I think it is a good bill. It makes a lot of sense. It is timely. It is relevant and it fits the times. It would change the Citizenship Act of this country. It reads:
I swear (or affirm) that I will be faithful and bear true allegiance to Canada and the Constitution of Canada, and that I will faithfully observe the laws of Canada and fulfil my duties as a Canadian citizen.
New citizens can relate to that. They have come to a new country and a new home. They are pledging allegiance to their new land. It is a public and solemn commitment to Canada. It is something that new Canadians want to do. It is part of a contact, so to speak. In acquiring a new home, the new citizen is swearing allegiance to it. It is part of a bonding process.
One might ask what is wrong with the old oath. It reads: "I swear or affirm that I will be faithful and bear true allegiance to Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II, Queen of Canada, Her heirs and successors, and that I will faithfully observe the laws of Canada and fulfil my duties as a Canadian citizen".
What is wrong? With all due respect to the British parliamentary system, which is one of the best in the world, the Queen, Her family and the monarchy are not that relevant to most new Canadians. In fact, they are not that relevant to most Canadians who have lived here all their lives.
That may sound odd coming from someone like me who would preserve the monarchy, certainly its infrastructure, if not every tiny aspect of it. The fact is that the monarchy is a distant institution. Sure, it is an important part of our Constitution. It serves a distinct governmental role that I support but there is almost no emotional attachment.
Yes, our Queen is our head of state but she does not live here. She is British. She is from far away. She comes to Canada for visits only. It is hardly the stuff on which to build emotional attachments.
I really wish that this were not true because, to repeat, I support the monarchy. If we did not have one, we would have to invent one. If only the Queen were here, if only she were a Canadian living in Canada the year round, that would make a big difference. That is not going to happen yet I have no stomach for severing our connection to the monarchy.
Therefore, I think we ought to amend some of our laws and one of them should be the Citizenship Act as proposed by this private member's bill.
Think about it. Having a new Canadian swear an oath of allegiance to Canada is exactly what the new citizen wants. It is direct, meaningful and it expresses the solemn commitment the citizen wants to make to Canada. It will not be damaging to the monarchy. It can easily survive this change because its basic structure would remain well intact.
None of this is far fetched. The Department of the Secretary of State back in 1987 kicked around some ideas for a new wording of the oath. One suggestion was: "I swear or affirm that I will be a loyal citizen of Canada, obey its laws, abide by its Constitution and faithfully fulfil my other citizenship duties".
March 18, 1993

To be frank, the current requirement is confusing to many new citizens, especially those who do not have a British Commonwealth background. They come to Canada and want to pledge allegiance to the country of their choice but they are left confused by having to swear an oath to the Queen. They cannot really understand why they are required to swear an oath to the Queen who is a person who resides in another country. It must be a bit disorienting.
The member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace told a story about a man who balked at taking the current oath. He felt that he had not chosen Britain but Canada. One man even took the government to court and argued, among other things, that the current act is unconstitutional. He lost. That aside, we can still do better.
It could be argued that the new citizens should learn our system of government and that would clear away the confusion and that is a valid point. Nevertheless, the new citizen wants to make his or her pledge directly to Canada. What better way is there than the one proposed by this private member's bill? I will repeat it:
I swear (or affirm) that I will be faithful and bear true allegiance to Canada and the Constitution of Canada, and that I will faithfully observe the laws of Canada and fulfil my duties as a Canadian citizen.
This proposed change to the act is just one more step in the growing up of Canada. Since our colonial status we have come a long way. We have a bit of a way to go and this change to the Citizenship Act should help. Along the way we acquired a new flag, an anthem, we stopped appointing non-Canadians as governors general about 40 years ago and we abolished legal appeals to the British Privy Council about the same time. It seems strange but until then our Supreme Court of Canada was really not the supreme court. Canadian citizenship did not come along until the 1940s and we were not able to amend our Constitution without British approval until the early 1980s. We all remember the big fight over our patriation of the Constitution.
We have come a long way as a country. Changing the Citizenship Act helps fill in the new face of Canada.
The bill bears a similarity to one I introduced in Parliament a couple of years ago. That bill, aimed at
Private Members' Business
changing the Parliament of Canada Act, would require parliamentarians to take an oath of allegiance to Canada and its Constitution. I do not think it is good enough for us to swear an oath to the Queen as the Constitution currently requires. It suits the constitutional niceties but there is a new pride in Canada and the people want their representatives to swear allegiance to Canada. The name Canada is important. They also want the oath to Canada because they know that from time to time people are elected to this House whose commitment to Canada is questionable. Voters want it on the record that every MP has taken an oath to Canada. Allegiance to the Queen is okay but adding an oath to our country firms up the commitment.
We have to take into account that there is a new spirit out there. It is a deep love for Canada and people want it reflected it in our laws, in our symbols and in our institutions. That is why I support this private member's bill and I hope that everyone in this House can do the same.
I believe that the bill should go to committee where possible improvements can be considered. Maybe room can be made in the bill for Canada, the Constitution and the Queen. In other words, it will have all three major elements. That may be seen as a compromise, but whatever the case this bill takes us in the right direction and it deserves our support.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Worthy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, very briefly, the bill that we are debating is Bill C-285, a private member's bill to change the Citizenship Act which affects the oath of allegiance.
With all the respect that I have for the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, I cannot support this bill.
I listened with interest though to the previous speaker. I think it will show the differences that we have in this country. It is one of the beautiful things about Canada that we do have the right to disagree on so many basic issues. Maybe it is my grey hair showing, but I have a terrible fondness for the history that the monarchy of this country represents. It goes beyond just symbolism. This is a country where our country and all of our traditions are based on the history of a monarchy.

March 18, 1993
Private Members' Business
By affirming the oath of citizenship, new Canadians participate in a formal ceremony that is rooted in tradition. They have explicit vows and implicit commitments. There are official witnesses in attendance. In most cases families and friends attend. They share in the pride of the occasion. There are pictures taken and afterwards there is usually a social ceremony. It is a solemn occasion that befits a ceremony uniting a new citizen with the country of Canada.
The oath underlines that Canadian citizenship is not to be entered into lightly. In a different context, the oath that the new citizens take is exactly the same oath that is taken by any public servant. Anybody who serves in our Armed Forces takes exactly the same oath. Anybody who is in the RCMP has to take exactly the same oath. It is the oath that I took when I took on the responsibility of being a member of Parliament in this country. It is the same oath that the senators who reside in the other place take before taking their seat. In fact, it is the identical oath, Madam Speaker, that you took as you became a member of Parliament for Canada.
There was a Commitment to Canada project. This project occurred last year on Canada's 125th anniversary. It was a project with Canadians who had never taken the oath, because most Canadians never take the oath, of allegiance. They were bom here and they are not required to. Last year more than 1 million voluntarily, on their own, re-established their love and respect for the country by going through the oath-taking ceremony. It was taken symbolically, yes, but for most of them it was a very real and meaningful occasion.
New Canadians, after going through the swearing-in ceremony, describe it as being suitably impressive. During the official procedure they swear or affirm the oath of citizenship before a judge and in the presence of a uniformed member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Of course they sing O Canada at the same time. They receive both a certificate and a commemorative document attesting to their new status as a Canadian citizen. An American, who became a Canadian citizen recently, called the ceremony:
a lovely affair with just the right amount of pomp. There were 105 of us there, from 28 countries. And when, at the end, the judge read out the list of countries, I knew why I was there and why I was a
Canadian. The catalogue of countries was a poem of people coming home to a new place. The old countries were still there, on the globe and in our lives, for most of us had not escaped from something; we had simply come to another place that let us be ourselves without having to melt like cheese in a rusty pot.
Canadians understand that swearing allegiance to the Queen of Canada is not the same as swearing or affirming allegiance to a foreign power.
There was a paper "Proud to be Canadian" which was circulated in the previous term, 1987-88 and a great many people responded to it. Interestingly enough, the subject of the Queen and the oath generated the largest public reaction, mostly through letters. On the consultations carried out afterwards based on this discussion paper, "Proud to be Canadian", the majority of the people spoken to indicated support for retaining the Queen in the oath of citizenship. In contrast, only a few people wanted the Queen excluded from the oath.
At that time, a major point was made that the Queen is what distinguishes us in many cases from becoming an American. Deletion would be denying the reality of our country's membership in the Commonwealth. The Queen is viewed as a symbol of unity and is part of our historical tie.
I received a copy of a letter which was addressed to the hon. member who is proposing this amendment. It is from the Canadian Citizenship Federation. In that letter an appeal is made to the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace that he desist from continuing his motion. I will quote: "We wish to take this opportunity to record in the strongest possible terms our unanimous objection to the proposal contained in Bill C-285, to amend the oath of allegiance as described in the current Citizenship Act".
The argument the people put forward in opposition to this amendment centre around the fact that the Queen is still a fundamental part of our system of government. Canada is a constitutional monarchy. The presence of the Queen in the person of the Governor General provides a balance in the organization of our government that is vital to its democratic operation. To remove reference to the Queen in the oath of allegiance would be to deny this fundamental truth.
March 18, 1993

If you are going to change the oath of loyalty to the Queen then in effect you really are going to be required to change the whole system. The people in the Canadian Citizenship Federation are very much opposed to that. They close their correspondence to the hon. member by again saying: "We implore you to withdraw your support of Bill C-285, an act to amend the Citizenship Act".
I would like to close by reading the oath all new Canadians make.
I swear that I will be faithful and bear true allegiance to Her
Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II, Queen of Canada, Her heirs and
successors, and that I will faithfully observe the laws of Canada and
fulfil my duties as a Canadian citizen.
Millions of Canadians have taken that oath, Madam Speaker. I have taken that oath, you have taken that oath. I will not support the amendment proposed by the hon. member.

Madam Speaker, I believe that we need to move with caution in making a change to the oath of citizenship and not move with the haste that the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace suggests.
We are talking about making a change that in isolation may appear on the surface to be minor. Yet in reality, the change would have a far-reaching impact, an impact not only on the oath of citizenship but on oaths administered to members of the House, the other place, members of the Armed Forces and of course the Public Service.
An oath of allegiance to the monarch has been a staple of the Canadian naturalization or citizenship process since the year 1868. In the first years after Confederation anyone who wished to become naturalized as a British subject in Canada was required to take both an oath of residence and an oath of allegiance before the naturalization could become effective.
A person naturalized under this act was a British subject while in Canada but was not recognized as such outside Canada. When a husband acquired the status of a British subject, his wife became a British subject as well.
The Imperial Naturalization Act became effective January 1, 1915. Naturalization of aliens under this act was recognized throughout the world, bringing uniformi-
Private Members' Business
ty to the various naturalization acts in effect in the United Kingdom and in the Commonwealth. Again, an oath of allegiance to the monarch was sworn before naturalization could become effective.
As we are all aware, any person naturalized in Canada before January 1, 1947 became a British subject only and not a Canadian citizen.
The adoption of a distinctive Canadian Citizenship Act, the first of its kind in the British Commonwealth, came about as the result of increasing agitation during the 1930s and particularly during and immediately after World War II. After the adoption of the Statute of Westminster in 1931 there was a feeling that the people of Canada should have the official status of Canadian citizens and that there should be legislation covering it.
In 1946 the then Secretary of State, the Hon. Paul Martin, introduced a bill in the House which became the Canadian Citizenship Act effective January 1, 1947. After that date Canadian citizenship could be acquired by birth, prior naturalization or marriage and by British subjects who lived in Canada.
It is worth noting that this evolution did not affect the oath of allegiance. The oath was still required before Canadian citizenship could become effective.
After February 15, 1977 every qualified person applying for citizenship whether British, Irish or a member of a Commonwealth country, or indeed an alien, has had to take the oath of citizenship before acquiring Canadian citizenship and that is as it should be. The law applies equally with none of the previous preferential treatment for those legally domiciled in Canada from Britain, Ireland and Commonwealth countries.
Thus we have had oaths swearing allegiance to the Crown in Canada for more than 125 years. It is absolutely clear that the allegiance being sworn is to the Queen of Canada. Canada is a constitutional monarchy, as my colleague said who just spoke before me.
It will remain so until a constitutional amendment agreed to by the federal government and all the provincial governments provide otherwise. Our Constitution spells out very clearly that the Queen embodies a democratic system of Canadian government encompassing the House of Commons, the Senate and the Governor General.

March 18, 1993
Private Members' Business
Thus when people swear the oath of citizenship it is to a concept of Canada that we all share. The oath of citizenship is a part of that system. The wording reflects our constitutional monarchy and acknowledges our national heritage. To be a Canadian citizen is to accept and to recognize that legacy. This amendment would jettison that legacy.
As one hon. member commented when this bill was before the Elouse previously, this country has a long tradition of continuous association with the institution of the monarchy, beginning as far back as 1535 when Jacques Cartier claimed this area on behalf of the French crown.
As Canadians we have adapted the symbols from other parliamentary systems to make a strong Canadian parliamentary system and a strong democracy. The oath of citizenship is part of that system.
I also believe that changes to the oath at this time would prove most divisive. All amendments to the Citizenship Act, including possible changes to the oath of allegiance, should be considered in a comprehensive manner when the government introduces a series of amendments to make the act more contemporary.
The change proposed by this bill could hardly come at a more inappropriate time. Thousands of Canadians, especially young Canadians, are about to take the oath as their reaffirmation of Canadian citizenship during National Citizenship Week, which is April 11 to 17.1 will be attending one of those ceremonies in my riding and I am sure other hon. members will be doing the same.
During National Citizenship Week many members will participate in these citizenship ceremonies right across our country. These events will occur from coast to coast and in the far north as well. They will be in such varied locales as primary and secondary schools, citizenship courts, community halls and other gathering places.
In the schools, children will reaffirm their citizenship. In some instances, some of the teachers will take the oath of citizenship as well.
As many of us can attest, these ceremonies are joyous and touching occasions. For new Canadians, it is affirmation that they are accepted as equals and with the full responsibilities that come with citizenship in this great country of ours.
For those reaffirming their citizenship, it is confirmation that they are citizens, citizens of a nation that cherishes its heritage and yet builds for its future through the process of accepting people from around the world as Canadians and members of our wonderful society.
The board of the Canadian Citizenship Federation, which promotes the respect for and the recognition of Canadian symbols and traditions, believes the current oath of citizenship should remain unchanged.
In addition, the board members are of the unanimous position that not only the formality, but the dignity of the existing citizenship court ceremonies must be maintained and supported. It is their view that: "Without question, the solemnity and demeanour of the court proceedings creates a lasting feeling of respect and pride among new Canadian citizens."
In conclusion, let me restate my position. I oppose the amendment to change the current oath of citizenship because, first, the change is being made in isolation and not as part of a review of the entire Citizenship Act.
Second, I do not believe that something that is part of the heritage of every person who has become a Canadian citizen should be dismissed without serious public debate.
Third, as long as Canada remains a constitutional monarchy, I have severe and serious reservations about changing the oath of citizenship.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this important debate concerning the heritage of Canada and in particular the change that is proposed.
I had the privilege of being an immigrant to Canada many years ago. I came to a country that I was not familiar with. I heard suggested earlier in the debate by another member that new citizens swear allegiance to the Queen, yet think that as new Canadians the Queen is really irrelevant to their coming to Canada.
That may be true. I am sure they did not come to Canada because Canada was headed by a Queen. They came to Canada because of the many things that Canada had to offer. But to suggest that they did not come here because the Queen was here, therefore we should remove the Queen from the oath, I must admit I have some great difficulty with that.
March 18. 1993

It goes a little further because many of the traditions that we as Canadians have known are subject to change. We understand that and some of those changes are very appropriate. I might suggest that all of us as Canadians at one point or another have had to swear an oath, and in the past it was necessary to swear an oath on a Bible. A Bible is not the appropriate book for all Canadians because there are Canadians who have other holy books that they would prefer to use. We understand that and we changed to accommodate particular needs.
Whether we swear allegiance to the Queen or not is really not an affront to any person's individual beliefs or persuasions in a religious sense. Those who wanted to come to Canada and investigated coming here did so knowing full well that we had a parliamentary system with a tremendous heritage relating back to the British parliamentary system, which is headed by the Queen.
We all know we are members of the British Commonwealth throughout the world, and again that Commonwealth is headed by the Queen.
For those new Canadians who come to Canada and take exception to it, if that is the only exception they ever take to Canada then they have truly come to a very great place. I do not think that is a reason for those of us who believe in this oath to change.
Very clearly the amendment that is before the House today pays attention only to one small portion of the Citizenship Act, which is a very broad piece of legislation that serves all Canadians. Merely changing the oath, which has far-reaching implications for Canadians, is really to tinker with a piece of legislation that should be dealt with in its entirety. Everything should be looked at if we are going to adjust things, and unfortunately this piece of legislation before us does not do so. It takes a very piecemeal approach.
I do not believe the issue of the Citizenship Act is dormant. The government is examining the current act and the most visible aspect of the scrutiny has been the consultations the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship held with citizens and groups across Canada. This will lead to a reassessment of the act. That is
Private Members' Business
probably good, and hopefully will lead to a new citizenship act. It would be far better to deal with the issue of the actual oath when we address the broader and bigger concerns associated with Canadian citizenship and the Citizenship Act.
Canadian citizenship implies certain responsibilities. We often hear about the rights of citizens but for citizens there are responsibilities to; it is much more than the oath new Canadians or Canadians in general who are reaffirming their citizenship proclaim when swearing allegiance. The citizenship ceremony is symbolic. It is the final step new Canadians take in accepting their new home and accepting and acknowledging the rights and responsibilities of their citizenship.
All members in this House have participated in citizenship courts as members of Parliament. We have been invited to bring greetings and welcome new Canadians in our ridings. Those new Canadians who have sworn that oath of allegiance do so with all the pride and vigour that they can muster, at least that is true in the ones I participated in and I suspect the same is true in the ones you have been in, Madam Speaker.
They are not concerned in that context of the oath. Their pride is in becoming Canadian citizens.
I must place my reservations on record about the amendment to the oath of allegiance within the Citizenship Act as proposed by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace. This amendment addresses the symbolic aspect of the Citizenship Act rather than the broader issues of the act itself and as such should be seen as truly a half measure.
I might give some examples of why I think it is simply addressing a symbolic issue and is a half measure.
Canada has parliamentary traditions, no doubt about that. We believe that at the head of the Government of Canada there is the Queen and representing the Queen in Canada is the Governor General. If, as one of the members had suggested, the Queen is not important in the swearing of allegiance, then because many Canadians do not relate to the Governor General are we suggesting that we should remove the Governor General from our governmental process? I do not think so. I certainly hope not.

March 18, 1993
Private Members' Business
Every time the Government of Canada or the provincial governments are in the courts they are acting on behalf of the Crown. Are we proposing that we eliminate the Crown from any discussions, and that we get away from those traditions? I certainly hope not.
I mentioned before that like all new Canadians I had the privilege of taking that oath of allegiance and swearing my allegiance to the Queen. I also swore it when I was elected to the municipal council many years ago in Ajax and similarly here as a member of Parliament. This oath permeates many things that we do in Canada. There was a great uproar recently in Ontario when the police removed the oath of allegiance. It was very clear that according to the tradition of the police department it wanted to retain its oath, its promise, and its swearing of allegiance to the Queen.
I should point out that when I was a little smaller than I am today, in my early years as a boy scout, I made a promise to do my duty first to God and then to the Queen. Are we proposing that boy scouts should no longer promise to do their duty to the Queen because we do not like the mention of the Queen in an oath? I certainly hope not.
What I am trying to say in those comments is that the aspect of the Queen permeates Canadian society. To simply remove her at the first step, which is our oath of allegiance, may ripple all the way down through the system. I, for one, am certainly not interested in doing that.
I say "I for one" because I am pleased that earlier the member for Cariboo-Chilcotin talked about a group of citizens, the Canadian Citizenship Federation, and he quoted from a letter that had been addressed to a member of Parliament. From that letter it was very clear that there are a lot of Canadians who are opposed to this bill before the House. I am pleased to see that some of the members of that association are watching this debate. I welcome them and hope they are finding it interesting and very educational to hear the different views on the subject matter.
The basic rights and fundamental freedoms of our citizens are clearly laid out in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I reiterate for hon. members that
this government of which we are all members continues to pursue the fundamental values of Canadian citizenship that have a direct impact on our daily lives. Those values are equality and participation.
Within the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship there are several areas. There is the race relations and cross-cultural understanding branch to try to address concerns that are out there. Heritage cultures and language programs are being addressed. There are community support and participation programs, a multiculturalism secretariat, a human rights directorate, a voluntary action program, literacy and citizenship.
I did not leave citizenship to the last because it was least important but because all those previous items lead up to the most important aspect, and that is citizenship.
Madam Speaker, you are indicating that my time is running to an end. I do have several more comments but maybe I will have to return at some other point on this matter to discuss them. Very clearly, I believe we have enough activity in Canada to encourage citizenship. I believe the bill before us would not be conducive to strengthening citizenship in this country.

Madam Speaker, to begin I want to clearly lay on the record the fact that I will not support Bill C-285.
To explain why is simple: The intent of this bill is to remove all references to the Queen or the monarchy. I simply cannot accept that.
I want to be very specific about what the bill calls upon us to do in regard to the changing of the oath of allegiance. I will read into the record what this bill proposes to do. It says:
Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
1. The Schedule to the Citizenship Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
Oath or Affirmation of Citizenship
I swear (or affirm) that I will be faithful and bear true allegiance to Canada and the Constitution of Canada, and that I will faithfully observe the laws of Canada and fulfil my duties as a Canadian citizen.
That is what Bill C-285 proposes to do in taking away reference to the Queen and the monarchy. To put it into perspective I want to read into the record what the present citizenship oath states:
March 18, 1993

I swear (affirm) that I will be faithful and bear true allegiance to Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, Queen of Canada, Her heirs and successors and that I will faithfully observe the laws of Canada and fulfil my duties as a Canadian citizen.
I do not know what is to be gained by taking away reference to the Queen and the monarchy. We are a constitutional monarchy. We do affirm our allegiance to the Queen, as has been mentioned by just about every member in this House when taking our oath of office as members of Parliament. What is to be gained by this? I suggest absolutely nothing. But a whole lot can be lost, a lot of our history and a lot of our pride as Canadians.
One of the most touching things that happened to me as a member of Parliament was last fall when all members of this House and in fact all Canadian citizens were involved in the referendum debate. That was a gut-wrenching exercise to say the least, regardless of what side of that issue one was on. It was a very emotional debate. It was one in which every Canadian citizen had a chance to take part and many of them did. In fact, we had a huge voter turn out and Canadians had a chance to speak.
One of the things that touched me during that debate was something that happened in my own family. Until October 1992 my wife was an American citizen. She could not vote in the 1988 election. She could not help get me elected as a member of Parliament. In fact, I was a little bit concerned as to whether or not she would actually vote for me in 1988, so I was not too concerned at the time whether or not she had her Canadian citizenship.
All joking aside, it was a very proud moment for me when my wife wanted to become a Canadian citizen so that she could take part in that very worth-while debate in the fall of 1992. When she decided that she wanted to become a Canadian citizen she had absolutely no problem in taking the oath of citizenship because it is something that has been expected of all Canadians. Twenty-seven million Canadians appear to have no problem with that oath as it now exists.
One of the things that strikes me as a former teacher, as an educator in one of my previous lives, and I have had a few previous lives, is that as Canadians we do not have a real sense of the history of our country as citizens of other countries do. We have no sense of pride and nationhood as some countries have. In fact, that is one of our identity problems as a country.
Private Members' Business
There are only 27 million Canadians on the North American continent of over 300 million people. We are small in comparison to our American neighbours next door and the Mexicans. One of the things I have witnessed for many years is that the Americans have this intense sense of who they are and what they are. That has been missing in Canada.
Going back to my teaching days I always went to great lengths to try to instil in the minds of young Canadians what Canada was all about so that we would know ourselves. That is because we are infiltrated in Canada every single day, 365 days a year by, media messages, much of them spilling over from other countries, namely the United States of America.
I have often stated that in some ways Canadians are more familiar with the American anthem than they are with their own. We have a better understanding of their system of government than we do of our own system of government. We all have to take responsibility for not having promoted our side of the story over the years. We could have done more in that regard. I attempted to do that in my teaching days.
There is nothing wrong with a little nationalism. There is nothing wrong with a love of country and an understanding of how we evolved as a country. There is nothing wrong in understanding how the monarchy as it pertains to Britain and transplanted to Canada has evolved over the years, right from the days of the Magna Carta on up through. It is a very rich history. It is one that we can be very proud of as Canadians. I do not think it is one from which we want to dissociate ourselves.
Therefore I think Bill C-285 should not be considered by this House. However, let us put some of the numbers in perspective. I mentioned my own family situation and what my wife did last year in becoming a new Canadian. She is not alone in that. In fact last year more than one

March 18, 1993
Private Members' Business
million Canadians affirmed their citizenship as part of the 125th anniversary of Canadian Confederation.
Canada is the most sought after country in the world. What I mean by that is simply that it is the most desirable country to enter. Of course we have an ongoing debate as to how many people we should allow into Canada and how many the economy can sustain and how the country will grow, but that is a debate for another time.
The fact is that Canada is one of the most desirable countries in the world. Of those hundreds of thousands of people on this very day who wish to come to Canada, not a single person in my mind would have a problem in taking this oath of allegiance as it now stands.
Canada has been identified by the rest of the world as the number one best country in the world. There is none better. How did the rest of the world arrive at that conclusion? The world itself, the 162 countries that do belong to the United Nations, actually measured the well-being of their citizens. In doing that they measured and examined everything. They examined health care, they examined educational levels, access to universities and access to health care and support programs for seniors and disabled citizens. They even examined our charter of rights and the rights and freedoms we enjoy as Canadians. At the end of the day they concluded that Canada is indeed the best country in the entire world.
Well if we are good enough for the rest of the world, why can we not be good enough for ourselves? Why can we not just simply stand up and say: "Listen, what we have here is pretty good. Let us sustain it. Let us keep it". Why do we have to enter this debate to change something most of us readily accept?
The argument to change it is very shallow and does not deserve the merit and support of this House. Let us for once maintain the status quo. Let us maintain that which we consider to be truly Canadian. Therefore, I will not support Bill C-285. Madam Speaker, thank you very much for your understanding.

Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to speak on this particular private member's bill, but not because I am in favour of it.
I find that this bill lacks any kind of understanding of the true value of the Queen in our society. The Queen is our head of state and is personified in Canada through
the Governor General's office and the Lieutenant Governors in each individual province. Through these people and through this institution a tremendous amount of value is given to this particular country. It is something that people when they become new citizens learn to recognize by taking that oath of citizenship.
I come from a riding in metropolitan Toronto that is about 60 per cent immigrant and in which the number of people of British descent is very much a minority. Only about 18,000 people in Don Valley North list British as their heritage.
The people in my riding strongly value the Queen. I have attended many different events in the Vietnamese community, in the Hungarian community and in other communities at which a lieutenant governor has been present. I have seen people such as Pauline McGibbon, Lincoln Alexander and Henry Jackman using their particular office to help new citizens. They help citizens of Canada from all backgrounds to recognize the importance of that particular office and of its value in our country. It has nothing to do with a particular person, the Queen, although I think that Queen Elizabeth has been a tremendous queen. It is head of state and it is a non-political head of state.
One can go to something like the Hungarian ball and hear Lieutenant Governor Hal Jackman talking about Canada and about the values that we share as Canadian citizens. Lincoln Alexander at a high school in a suburban area of Toronto used that office to explain in a non-political way the value of our country. I think what a tremendous asset it is that we have this institution. It makes a tremendous amount of sense to have new citizens recognize that.
Many of these new citizens are fleeing countries because of the the lack of solid institutions such as the monarchy which we have and value in Canada. Looking at Canada, one of our main assets is these strong institutions. We have a civil service in which the value of a high-quality civil service and lack of corruption are held in extremely high regard.
Similarly in our Parliament, members of Parliament who act in a fraudulent way or break laws are held in tremendous disregard. In this country we have values that are very strongly held. In other countries it is frequently found that there is a level of understanding of the importance of institutions such as the police, such as an impartial justice system a non-political system in which people can come before their various institutions
March 18, 1993

no matter what their particular political persuasion is and find they are treated as individuals.
That is something that is a tremendous asset in Canada and is undervalued by many Canadian citizens. They do not recognize this to the same degree others do. It is an institution that has changed as Canada has changed.
We see the various representatives of the Queen and the Queen herself as being very much in touch with many of the issues we experience in Canada. They are very much aware of things such as racism and the problems of new citizens coming into our society. These are not people who are out of touch.
It is not a stuffy monarchy, an institution that has not kept pace with the changes in Canada. This has been reviewed before the courts. I have with me today one of the decisions with respect to the oath of citizenship.
There was a case involving Charles C. Roach who claimed that he was entitled to be granted citizenship without having to take the oath of citizenship in its present form.
He too was confusing the institution of the Queen and of the monarchy with a person. I will just read part of what Mr. Justice Joyal ruled: "It is in my view quite proper for Parliament to require persons wishing to become Canadian citizens that they swear and affirm their loyalty to the head of state. That the head of state should be found in the person of Her Majesty the Queen might be a matter of debate but it is nevertheless as much a part of our constitutional framework as are provisions of our chapter.
Furthermore, the personified symbol of Her Majesty as head of state is not in terms of our long constitutional heritage a latter day invention of some imaginative or manipulative spinner of tales, but the the result of constantly evolving constitutional principles which are cloaked in constitutional conventions in the United Kingdom and partly codified in Canada in the Constitution Act, 1982.
The head of state as Her Majesty is so defined is the very embodiment of the freedoms and liberties which the appellant has inherited and which he now enjoys.
Private Members' Business
In a legal sense, the head of state legitimizes the laws of Canada which in concrete terms provide for the peace, the order and the good government of its citizens.
The argument raised by the appellant that Canada's head of state is the Queen, that she is Anglican is evidence to me of a dialectic which is bereft of any legal or constitutional content".
This particular individual who challenged this oath of citizenship was making the same mistake as the member who sponsored this bill has made. He is confusing the particular person with the institution. The judge has affirmed the whole constitutional value of this in his statements. The office is in fact symbolic of our institutions and I think that is very, very important.
He also says: "Similarly, if the appellant feels that it is against his conscience to make oaths to all but the Supreme Being or to the principles of truth, freedom, equality, justice and the rule of law, the statute does not impose an oath of allegiance. Indeed out of respect for individual conscience an affirmation of allegiance will do as well".
There is flexibility within the oath of citizenship. I for one and the vast majority of my constituents and as I say a very multicultural constituency, strongly believe that an oath of citizenship with the enunciation of the Queen as the head of state is very important and something that we all value as Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I, like a number of my colleagues who have spoken before, do not feel that it is appropriate that I should be supporting this legislation.
Before I go into my prepared remarks which talk about the history of the oath, I would like to preface my comments with some off the cuff words on how, in listening to previous speakers, this debate has caught me a little bit off guard. I did not really think that I would have the emotional impact of what I have heard earlier. I say that with a lot of sincerity.
At a time in our country and even internationally when change keeps coming at us from various directions, and it is coming on us on a regular basis, we keep looking for what our roots are and where we could stabilize ourselves. We can do that within our own family unit. We can do that within our church and our beliefs. We can do that within our institutions.
